column2: climate change monetary policy
column3:
Climate change affects monetary policy through the transmission mechanism, the appropriate policy stance, and the design of monetary-policy instruments. Climate-related developments can independently alter financial conditions—reinforcing or offsetting the monetary-policy stance—and can change how firms, households and financial intermediaries respond to that stance. These effects may become stronger as climate deterioration and the green transition advance, so they should be incorporated into the information used to assess monetary transmission. Asset prices are identified as one important channel. (Climate change and monetary policy.pdf, pp. 19–20)

Climate change also reduces trend output and increases the volatility of output and inflation, while physical climate events and transition measures can create cyclical shocks requiring a monetary-policy response. However, there is no “one size fits all” approach to determining the net effect on the policy stance. Climate risks and transition policies may also affect the neutral rate, but their overall impact remains unclear. The investment needs of the green transition materially affect investment dynamics; carbon-related taxes may create short-term costs, while the shift to renewables should ultimately reduce dependence on fossil-fuel imports and inflation volatility. The operational framework is also intended to incorporate climate considerations into structural monetary-policy operations. (Climate change and monetary policy.pdf, p. 29)

column2: climate change monetary policy
column3:
Climate change affects monetary policy through three main channels. First, it can weaken or otherwise alter monetary-policy transmission by independently changing financial conditions and by changing how firms, households and financial intermediaries respond to the policy stance. Asset prices are one important transmission channel. These effects may become more significant as climate deterioration and the green transition progress, so climate factors should be incorporated into the information used to assess transmission. (Climate change and monetary policy.pdf, pp.19–20)

Second, physical climate events and transition measures can create macroeconomic shocks, increasing output and inflation volatility, while climate risks and transition policies may also affect the neutral interest rate. Their combined effect on the appropriate monetary-policy stance is uncertain, meaning there is no single response applicable to every climate-related shock. The green transition also materially affects investment dynamics; although carbon-related taxes may impose short-term costs, greater use of renewables should ultimately reduce dependence on fossil-fuel imports and inflation volatility. (Climate change and monetary policy.pdf, p.29) Finally, climate-related considerations are intended to be incorporated into the design of structural monetary-policy operations. (Climate change and monetary policy.pdf, p.29)

column2: ECB climate
column3:
The ECB expects banks to prudently manage and transparently disclose climate-related and environmental risks under current prudential rules. Its final guide applied immediately from 27 November 2020. The ECB planned self-assessments and action plans in early 2021, followed by supervisory benchmarking and dialogue; a full supervisory review and follow-up measures were planned for 2022. It also announced a 2022 supervisory stress test focused on climate-related risks and identified weaknesses in banks’ climate-risk disclosures, particularly the lack of relevant quantitative and qualitative information. (ECB publishes final guide on climate-related and environmental risks for banks.pdf, p.1)

ECB-related climate-risk analytical tools include climate beta, CRISK, Carbon Value at Risk, climate spreads, and normalised or collateral-adjusted exposure-at-risk. These measures address, respectively, sensitivity of asset prices, climate-conditional capital shortfalls, securities’ exposure to future carbon-price changes, climate-related financing-cost differences, and expected losses from physical risks. (Assessment of Climate-related Vulnerabilities_ Analytical framework and toolkit.pdf, p.28) More recently, the ECB decided in July 2025 to introduce a climate factor to protect Eurosystem collateral against climate-related transition shocks, applicable from 15 June 2026 to marketable assets issued by non-financial corporations. It also postponed making compliance with the Corporate Sustainability Reporting Directive a collateral-eligibility criterion, citing incomplete national transposition and the Directive’s review. (Annual Report 2025.pdf, pp.108–109)

column2: What are the ECB's supervisory priorities?
column3:
For 2026–2028, the ECB’s supervisory priorities are to:

- **Strengthen banks’ resilience to geopolitical risks and macro-financial uncertainties**, including rising geopolitical tensions, trade fragmentation, climate- and nature-related risks, demographic change and rapid technological transformation. (Supervisory Priorities for 2026 - 2028 _ Management Solutions.pdf, p.1)
- **Strengthen operational resilience and ICT capabilities**, notably by addressing weaknesses in operational-resilience frameworks, IT outsourcing and IT-security/cyber risks. (Supervisory Priorities for 2026 - 2028 _ Management Solutions.pdf, p.1; ECB Banking Supervision_ SSM supervisory priorities for 2024-2026.pdf, p.3)
- **Advance digital transformation**, including the development of robust digital—and particularly AI-related—strategies supported by appropriate governance and risk-management frameworks. (Supervisory Priorities for 2026 - 2028 _ Management Solutions.pdf, p.1; Supervisory priorities 2026-28.pdf, pp.2–3)

These priorities are based on the latest SREP findings and are implemented through supervisory work programmes addressing the vulnerabilities identified. The ECB will also continue regular supervision, follow-up on past priorities and institution-specific risk work. (Supervisory Priorities for 2026 - 2028 _ Management Solutions.pdf, p.1; Supervisory priorities 2026-28.pdf, pp.2–3)

column2: ECB banking supervision
column3:
ECB Banking Supervision’s 2024–2026 priorities include assessing outsourcing arrangements and concentration risks through data collection and horizontal analysis of banks’ outsourcing registers. It will also conduct targeted reviews of outsourcing and cyber-resilience arrangements, complemented by targeted on-site inspections (OSIs) to identify institution-specific deficiencies. In addition, a thematic cyber-resilience stress test was planned to assess banks’ ability to respond to and recover from a successful cyberattack. (ECB Banking Supervision_ SSM supervisory priorities for 2024-2026.pdf, pp. 16–17)

The ECB is also increasing its focus on boards’ collective IT expertise, institutions relying on end-of-life systems supporting critical banking activities, outsourcing—including cloud outsourcing—and the monitoring of those arrangements. It expects full compliance with the applicable outsourcing requirements within the relevant timelines and is placing greater emphasis on ensuring that critical IT functions are assessed by internal IT audit. (Annual report on the outcome of the SREP IT Risk Questionnaire – Feedback to the industry.pdf, p. 4) In 2025, the ECB further pursued digitalisation of supervisory processes and completed implementation of the updated EBA reporting framework reflecting requirements from CRR III and CRD VI. (ECB Annual Report on supervisory activities 2025.pdf, pp. 63–64)

column2: ECB guide to internal models
column3:
The ECB Guide to Internal Models explains how the ECB understands and intends to apply the applicable EU and national rules when assessing whether institutions meet requirements for internal models. It is also intended for internal use by supervisory teams to promote a common and consistent supervisory approach, while allowing the ECB to consider each institution’s specific circumstances. (ECB guide to internal models.pdf, p.6)

The Guide is not intended to replace, override or extend applicable EU or national law, including adopted regulatory and implementing technical standards. It is also without prejudice to policy positions that the European Banking Authority may adopt under the CRR3. Some sections may require revision when further standards are finalised or adopted. (ECB guide to internal models.pdf, p.6) Its contents cover overarching principles, governance, documentation, data governance, validation, audit, climate-related and environmental risks, machine-learning techniques, model changes, third-party involvement and consolidations, as well as credit-risk topics such as the IRB approach and the definition of default. (ECB guide to internal models.pdf, p.3)

The excerpted publication is dated July 2025 and states that it has become outdated; it directs readers to the latest version on the ECB’s banking supervision website. (ECB guide to internal models.pdf, p.1)

column2: What are the FATF Recommendations?
column3:
The FATF Recommendations are an international standard for combating money laundering, terrorist financing, and the financing of proliferation. They are designed to be implemented by countries through measures adapted to their own legal, administrative, operational, and financial circumstances, rather than through identical measures in every country. (FATF Recommendations 2012 (updated 2023.11).pdf, p.8)

They set out essential measures to: identify risks and develop policies and domestic coordination; pursue money laundering, terrorist financing, and proliferation financing; apply preventive measures to the financial sector and other designated sectors; establish powers and responsibilities for competent authorities; improve the transparency and availability of beneficial-ownership information concerning legal persons and arrangements; and facilitate international cooperation. (FATF Recommendations 2012 (updated 2023.11).pdf, p.8) The original FATF Forty Recommendations were issued in 1990, revised in 1996, and expanded in 2001 to address terrorist financing through the creation of Eight, later Nine, Special Recommendations. (FATF Recommendations 2012 (updated 2023.11).pdf, p.8)

column2: FATF Recommendations
column3:
Les Recommandations du GAFI (FATF) constituent une norme internationale de lutte contre le blanchiment de capitaux, le financement du terrorisme et le financement de la prolifération des armes de destruction massive. Elles sont élaborées et promues par le Groupe d’action financière, organisme intergouvernemental indépendant chargé de protéger le système financier mondial contre ces menaces. (fatf-recommendations-2012.pdf, p.1-2)

Elles ne prescrivent pas des mesures identiques pour tous les pays : ceux-ci doivent les mettre en œuvre au moyen de mesures adaptées à leurs cadres juridiques, administratifs et opérationnels ainsi qu’à leurs systèmes financiers respectifs. Elles définissent notamment les mesures essentielles visant à identifier les risques et à développer des politiques ainsi qu’une coordination nationale, poursuivre le blanchiment de capitaux, le financement du terrorisme et le financement de la prolifération, appliquer des mesures préventives au secteur financier et aux autres secteurs désignés, établir les pouvoirs et responsabilités des autorités compétentes, améliorer la transparence et la disponibilité des informations sur les bénéficiaires effectifs des personnes morales et constructions juridiques, et faciliter la coopération internationale. (fatf-recommendations-2012.pdf, p.8)

Les quarante premières Recommandations ont été élaborées en 1990 pour lutter contre l’utilisation abusive des systèmes financiers à des fins de blanchiment de capitaux issus de la drogue. Elles ont été révisées en 1996, puis le mandat du GAFI a été étendu en octobre 2001 au financement des actes et organisations terroristes, avec l’adoption de huit, puis neuf, Recommandations spéciales sur le financement du terrorisme. (fatf-recommendations-2012.pdf, p.8)

column2: FATF AML/CFT
column3:
The **Financial Action Task Force (FATF)** is an independent intergovernmental body that develops and promotes policies to protect the global financial system against **money laundering (ML), terrorist financing (TF), and the financing of proliferation of weapons of mass destruction (PF)**. Its Recommendations are recognised as the global **anti-money-laundering (AML) and counter-terrorist-financing (CFT) standard**. (FATF-4th-Round-Procedures.pdf.coredownload.pdf, pp. 1–2)

The FATF’s fourth-round procedures establish the framework for **AML/CFT mutual evaluations**. The associated methodology assesses both **technical compliance with the FATF Recommendations** and the **effectiveness of AML/CFT/CPF systems**—where CPF means counter-proliferation financing. (FATF-4th-Round-Procedures.pdf.coredownload.pdf, pp. 1–2; FATF-Assessment-Methodology-2022.pdf, pp. 1–2) The excerpts do not identify a specific law, article, directive, or regulation as the legal basis for these standards.

column2: FATF high-risk jurisdictions
column3:
The FATF identifies and continually reviews jurisdictions with strategic deficiencies in their anti-money laundering, counter-terrorist financing and counter-proliferation-financing frameworks that pose risks to the international financial system. The process is overseen by the FATF’s International Co-operation Review Group (ICRG), which assesses jurisdictions according to threats, vulnerabilities or particular risks, and issues a public warning about risks emanating from identified jurisdictions. (Report on the State of Effectiveness and Compliance with the FATF Standards.pdf, p.12)

A jurisdiction must address all or nearly all elements of its ICRG action plan to be removed from FATF monitoring. The FATF has publicly identified more than 80 jurisdictions through this process, and more than 60 have made the necessary changes and exited the process. (Report on the State of Effectiveness and Compliance with the FATF Standards.pdf, p.13) The FATF’s list of high-risk and non-cooperative jurisdictions is one possible source for assessing a jurisdiction’s AML/CFT controls, but membership of the FATF or a FATF-style regional body does not, by itself, establish that a jurisdiction’s AML/CFT regime is adequate and effective. (EBA GL 2021 02 - consolidated (amended by EBA GL 2023 03)_EN.docx.pdf, p.19)

column2: FATF virtual assets
column3:
Under the FATF definition, a **virtual asset** is a digital representation of value that can be digitally traded or transferred and used for payment or investment. It excludes digital representations of fiat currencies, securities, and other financial assets already covered elsewhere under the FATF Recommendations. (FATF Recommendations 2012 (updated 2023.11).pdf, p.138)

A **virtual asset service provider (VASP)** is a natural or legal person not covered elsewhere under the FATF Recommendations that, as a business, conducts activities for or on behalf of another person. The excerpt specifically identifies: **(i)** exchange between virtual assets and fiat currencies, and **(ii)** exchange between one or more forms of virtual assets. (FATF Recommendations 2012 (updated 2023.11).pdf, p.138) FATF’s standards on virtual assets and VASPs form part of its broader global standards addressing money laundering, terrorist financing, and proliferation financing risks. (7th-targeted-update-on-implementation-fatf-standards-vas-vasps-2026.pdf, p.1-3)

column2: What are the transparency rules for non-equity instruments?
column3:
For non-equity instruments—bonds, structured finance products, emission allowances and derivatives—market operators and investment firms operating a trading venue must publish current bid and offer prices and the depth of trading interests at those prices. This information must be available continuously during normal trading hours, with requirements calibrated to different trading-system types under Annex I of Commission Delegated Regulation (EU) 2017/583 (RTS 2). Specific rules also apply to package orders and exchange-for-physical orders. (esma70-156-3329_mifid_ii_mifir_review_report_on_the_transparency_regime_for_non-equity_instruments.pdf, p.12; pp.12–13)

Pre-trade transparency waivers are available only in limited, clearly defined circumstances. They may cover orders that are large in scale compared with normal market size and orders held in a trading venue’s order management facility pending disclosure. Derivative transactions by non-financial counterparties are also exempt where they objectively reduce risks directly related to the commercial activity of the counterparty or its group. (esma70-156-3329_mifid_ii_mifir_review_report_on_the_transparency_regime_for_non-equity_instruments.pdf, p.12; pp.12–13) Post-trade, the price, volume and time of transactions executed in non-equity instruments must be made public as close to real time as technically possible—within 15 minutes during the first three years of application, and within 5 minutes thereafter. (esma70-156-3329_mifid_ii_mifir_review_report_on_the_transparency_regime_for_non-equity_instruments.pdf, p.32)

column2: What are the liquidity management tools under AIFMD?
column3:
The excerpts identify the following principal liquidity management tools under **Annex V of AIFMD**: **suspension of subscriptions, redemption gates, and side pockets**. A side pocket separates assets whose economic or legal characteristics have materially changed or become uncertain in exceptional circumstances from the fund’s other assets. (ESMA34-671404336-1345_Final_Report_on_the_Draft_Regulatory_Technical_Standards_on_open-ended_loan-originating_AIFs_under_the_AIFMD.pdf, pp. 21–22; cssf25_901_recueil_eng.pdf, p. 25)

Other tools reported in connection with open-ended funds include **lock-up periods**, **standby credit facilities**, **diversification of the investor base**, and **swing pricing**. Lock-up periods prevent redemptions for a predetermined period. However, **soft closures** and **extensions of settlement periods** may be available where appropriate but do **not** qualify as liquidity management tools within the meaning of AIFMD. (ESMA34-671404336-1345_Final_Report_on_the_Draft_Regulatory_Technical_Standards_on_open-ended_loan-originating_AIFs_under_the_AIFMD.pdf, pp. 21–22; cssf25_901_recueil_eng.pdf, p. 25)

column2: What are the CSDR settlement discipline rules?
column3:
The CSDR settlement-discipline regime is structured around three main measures for addressing settlement failures: **reporting settlement fails, cash penalties, and a mandatory buy-in regime**. It also includes measures to prevent failures—such as allocations and confirmations, automation, mandatory matching and relevant CSD functionalities—and monitoring of settlement fails. (2016-174_-_final_report_on_csdr_rts_on_settlement_discipline_0.pdf, pp.1–2; esma70-156-5011_final_report_-_rts_settlement_discipline_-_buy-in_suspension.pdf, p.5)

The regime entered into force on **1 February 2022**. However, market participants reported serious implementation difficulties with mandatory buy-ins. In response, the co-legislators agreed that the costs of mandatory buy-ins might outweigh their benefits and amended the framework to allow different application dates for the individual settlement-discipline measures, while the buy-in regime could be further assessed and potentially amended. (esma70-156-5011_final_report_-_rts_settlement_discipline_-_buy-in_suspension.pdf, p.5; esma70-156-5011_final_report_-_rts_settlement_discipline_-_buy-in_suspension.pdf, pp.12–13)

column2: ESMA MiFID II
column3:
ESMA’s MiFID II product-governance guidelines apply to firms and competent authorities involved in manufacturing or distributing financial instruments and structured deposits. They address requirements under MiFID II and the MiFID II Delegated Directive, including manufacturers’ and distributors’ product-governance obligations. The guidelines apply from two months after their publication on ESMA’s website in all EU official languages. (ESMA35-43-3448_Guidelines_on_product_governance.pdf, p.3)

The excerpts also describe ESMA proposals to integrate sustainability risks and factors into the MiFID II framework. In product governance, these proposals concern manufacturers’ and distributors’ definition and review of the target market, with ESG considerations or ESG preferences added to relevant delegated provisions. (esma35-43-1737_final_report_on_integrating_sustainability_risks_and_factors_in_the_mifid_ii.pdf, p.25) MiFID II is identified as Directive 2014/65/EU, while MiFIR is identified as Regulation (EU) No 600/2014. (esma70-156-3329_mifid_ii_mifir_review_report_on_the_transparency_regime_for_non-equity_instruments.pdf, p.8)

column2: What are the UCITS sustainability requirements?
column3:
UCITS management companies are expected to integrate sustainability risks into their organisational arrangements, investment decision-making and risk-management processes using a principles-based approach, similar to the treatment of other relevant risks. The framework should include effective and adequate procedures, appropriately skilled personnel, regular reviews and internal reporting, sufficient analytical, research and legal support, cooperation between relevant functions, and systems, processes and internal controls capable of identifying and analysing sustainability risks over time. Conflicts of interest arising from sustainability considerations must also be identified, prevented, managed and disclosed. (esma34-45-688_final_report_on_integrating_sustainability_risks_and_factors_in_the_ucits_directive_and_the_aifmd.pdf, p.10)

The governing body should be responsible for integrating sustainability risks and should periodically approve and review the risk-management policy, arrangements, processes, techniques and risk limits for each managed UCITS. The management company should employ sufficient personnel with the necessary skills, knowledge and expertise, taking account of the nature, scale and complexity of its business and services, as well as the resources and expertise needed for effective sustainability-risk integration. It should also maintain documented decision-making procedures and reporting lines, ensure that relevant persons understand their responsibilities, and operate adequate internal controls to ensure compliance with decisions and procedures. (esma34-45-688_final_report_on_integrating_sustainability_risks_and_factors_in_the_ucits_directive_and_the_aifmd.pdf, p.14–15)

column2: What are the revised SREP guidelines?
column3:
The revised SREP Guidelines are a single, comprehensive framework for the Supervisory Review and Evaluation Process (SREP), which consolidates supervisory findings into an overall assessment of an institution. They are addressed to competent authorities and also aim to harmonise supervisory stress testing across the EU. The revision reflects the banking package—Directive (EU) 2024/1619 and Regulation (EU) 2024/1623—as well as DORA (Regulation (EU) 2022/2554), the IRRBB/CSRBB package, and supervisory experience from almost a decade of implementation. (Final Report on revised SREP and supervisory stress testing Guidelines.pdf, p.5)

The revised framework retains the core SREP structure while adding ESG factors, operational resilience, third-country branches, and clarification of the interaction between revised Pillar 1 and Pillar 2 capital requirements, including the output floor. It integrates ICT risk assessment and repeals the separate ICT SREP Guidelines (EBA/GL/2017/05), with the aim of simplifying and improving consistency. It also strengthens proportionality, sequencing and supervisory effectiveness, including extending the assessment cycle for certain stable, low-risk Category 4 institutions from three to five years, subject to specified conditions. (Final Report on revised SREP and supervisory stress testing Guidelines.pdf, pp.5–6, 222–223) The guidelines further support risk-based supervision and require institutions to be categorised into four categories for proportionality, taking account of size, systemic importance, and the nature, scale and complexity of their activities. (Final Report on revised SREP and supervisory stress testing Guidelines.pdf, p.223)

column2: What are the EBA guidelines on ESG risk management?
column3:
The EBA’s ESG risk management guidelines broaden the focus beyond climate and environmental risks to cover environmental, social and governance risks more comprehensively. They set out supervisory expectations for integrating ESG risks into institutions’ strategies, business models, governance, operations, risk management and internal control systems. A central feature is the transition plan: institutions should use it as a concrete roadmap for managing ESG risks under the prudential framework. (Publication-EBA-Guidelines-vLinkedIn.pdf, p.1–2)

The guidelines expect institutions to conduct a materiality assessment, identify ESG risk transmission channels, scan the business environment, and analyse how material risks could affect their strategy and business model. These findings should support the definition of mitigation objectives and the transition plan, with robust ESG data underpinning the process. The guidelines build on EU and international requirements and principles, including BCBS principles and NGFS guidance, and cross-reference EBA requirements on loan origination and monitoring, internal governance, and Pillar 3 ESG risk metrics. (Publication-EBA-Guidelines-vLinkedIn.pdf, p.1–2; Final Guidelines on the management of ESG risks.pdf, p.12)

column2: EBA operational risk
column3:
The EBA’s operational-risk work focuses on implementing the new operational-risk framework—the **Standardised Measurement Approach (SMA)**—as part of the EU implementation of the **Basel III framework** under the **Banking Package**. Its priorities include supporting implementation in the EU, monitoring and promoting the consistent application of operational-risk requirements, and providing support through Q&A. (Single-Programming-Document-2026-2028-initial-1-1.pdf, p.40)

The planned ongoing output includes **technical standards on the exclusion of losses** (“RTS on the exclusion of losses”), scheduled for **Q1**. The excerpts do not specify a more detailed legal basis or particular provisions for this measure. (Single-Programming-Document-2026-2028-initial-1-1.pdf, p.40)

column2: EBA outsourcing guidelines
column3:
The **EBA Guidelines on outsourcing arrangements (EBA/GL/2019/02)** incorporate the earlier **EBA Recommendations on outsourcing to cloud service providers (EBA/REC/2017/03)**. They were intended to establish a consistent approach to outsourcing, including cloud outsourcing, across the banking sector and to support supervisory convergence. (8b80b926-ad14-48fc-9618-325234845d03_en.pdf, pp. 3–4, 33)

The ECB Banking Supervision expects institutions to comply fully with the applicable outsourcing requirements within the relevant timelines. Existing outsourcing arrangements were generally required to be documented in line with the Guidelines after the first renewal date, and no later than **31 December 2021**; this documentation requirement expressly excluded outsourcing arrangements to cloud service providers. (Annual report on the outcome of the SREP IT Risk Questionnaire – Feedback to the industry.pdf, p. 14) The excerpts do not provide the full detailed requirements of EBA/GL/2019/02, nor do they identify a specific legal basis beyond the Guidelines themselves.

column2: EBA Pillar 3 disclosures
column3:
The EBA’s final draft Implementing Technical Standards (ITS), published on 22 June 2026, amend the Pillar 3 disclosure framework to complete the disclosure requirements introduced by the revised Capital Requirements Regulation (CRR3). They revise ESG-risk disclosures and introduce new disclosure requirements for equity exposures and aggregate exposures to shadow banking entities, with the objectives of improving clarity, consistency and usability as part of the EU simplification agenda. (A&O Shearman _ FinReg _ EBA final draft ITS on amended Pillar 3 disclosures.pdf, p.1; EBA updates Pillar 3 disclosure requirements on ESG risks, equity and shadow banking exposures, as part of simplification effort _ European Banking Authority.pdf, p.1-2)

For ESG disclosures, the scope is extended beyond large listed institutions to large non-listed institutions, other institutions, small and non-complex institutions (SNCIs), and large subsidiaries. The framework is proportionate, with requirements differentiated according to an institution’s size and complexity. SNCIs would disclose only essential information, including physical and transition risks and exposures to fossil-fuel sectors, while requirements for larger institutions are clarified and streamlined rather than expanded. (A&O Shearman _ FinReg _ EBA final draft ITS on amended Pillar 3 disclosures.pdf, p.1; EU_ EBA publishes long-awaited final draft ITS amending the Pillar 3 disclosure framework on ESG risks, Premlata Fagan.pdf, p.1-2) The ESG Pillar 3 framework is closely linked to the EBA’s ESG supervisory-reporting framework under consultation and is aligned with the European Sustainability Reporting Standards (ESRS); the two documents should therefore be read together. (EBA updates Pillar 3 disclosure requirements on ESG risks, equity and shadow banking exposures, as part of simplification effort _ European Banking Authority.pdf, p.1-2)

column2: What is the ORSA under Solvency II?
column3:
The **ORSA (Own Risk and Solvency Assessment)** is a regular assessment that an insurance or reinsurance undertaking performs as part of its risk-management system. Its purpose is to identify and assess all risks inherent in the business and determine the undertaking’s **overall solvency needs**, including the amount and quality of own funds required for its particular risk exposure and business objectives. It must take a forward-looking view of the risks faced by the undertaking. (0ae6b432-4ca1-415c-8613-45407266f00b_en.pdf, p.15; p.8)

The ORSA reflects the undertaking’s risk profile, approved risk-tolerance limits and business strategy, and its results should inform management and strategic decisions, such as risk retention or transfer, capital management and premium-setting. It is not satisfied merely by producing a report or completing templates, and the undertaking cannot assume that regulatory capital requirements alone are sufficient for its specific risks. (0ae6b432-4ca1-415c-8613-45407266f00b_en.pdf, p.15)

column2: What are the Solvency II capital requirements?
column3:
The excerpts describe Solvency II capital requirements as requiring an undertaking to demonstrate that it can comply **continuously** with its regulatory capital requirements. This forward-looking assessment must consider potential material changes in its risk profile; the quantity and quality of own funds throughout the business-planning period; and the tier composition of own funds, including changes resulting from redemptions, repayments and maturities. (Final_EN_ORSA_Clean.pdf, p.9)

The undertaking must also assess whether its risk profile deviates significantly from the assumptions underlying the Solvency II **Solvency Capital Requirement (SCR)** calculation. A qualitative assessment may be used first, with quantitative assessment required where the deviation may be significant. (Final_EN_ORSA_Clean.pdf, p.9) The excerpts also indicate that capital requirements address major risks such as credit risk and issuer-level concentration risk, although they do not cover every vulnerability, particularly those associated with illiquid and difficult-to-value assets. (FINANCIAL STABILITY REPORT.pdf, p.89)

The excerpts do not provide the numerical capital thresholds, calculation formulas, or a complete breakdown of the Solvency II requirements. They also indicate that an internal model may be used in certain circumstances, but the undertaking must assess the position that its internal-model application could be rejected. (Final_EN_ORSA_Clean.pdf, p.5–6)

column2: EIOPA Solvency II
column3:
EIOPA is revising the Solvency II framework to support a sound and consistent application of the amended rules. Although Solvency II remains primarily microprudential, its macroprudential dimension has been strengthened. The reviewed framework introduces macroprudential considerations in the ORSA and PPP, requirements for short-, medium- and long-term liquidity plans, and further conditions under which competent authorities must act in response to macroprudential concerns. Improvements to quantitative reporting templates introduced from year-end 2023 also enhance liquidity monitoring. EIOPA has revised the related supervisory reporting and public disclosure technical standards, with the aim of significantly reducing insurers’ and reinsurers’ reporting burden. (FINANCIAL STABILITY REPORT.pdf, pp. 22–23)

EIOPA is also conducting a sequential review of all existing Solvency II guidelines, both to align them with the revised legal framework and to simplify and shorten them. The stated aim is to retain only what is strictly necessary for sound and consistent application. In the guidelines on related undertakings and participations, amendments update and clarify Guidelines 1, 2, 3, 6 and 7; Guideline 3 requires participating undertakings to demonstrate, through qualitative and quantitative assessment, that the equity investment is likely to be materially less volatile. Guideline 5 is deleted and partly incorporated into Guideline 4, while Guidelines 8 and 9 are deleted because the underlying legal provisions are considered sufficiently clear. (2f3549ce-6f73-4f89-a00d-712f86236105_en.pdf, p. 4) A separate set of amended guidelines, including Guidelines 1, 4, 5, 9, 12, 15, 16 and 23 and the technical annex, is scheduled to apply from 30 January 2027. (dda6cfcc-e3f0-4d40-91a4-b870dfb15522_en.pdf, pp. 3–4) EIOPA is also continuing work on implementing the European Insurance Recovery and Resolution Directive (IRRD). (FINANCIAL STABILITY REPORT.pdf, p. 23)

column2: EIOPA ORSA
column3:
EIOPA’s ORSA framework concerns the **forward-looking assessment of an undertaking’s own risks**, based on ORSA principles. EIOPA issued guidelines for National Competent Authorities during the preparatory phase for applying the Solvency II Directive, with the aim of promoting a consistent and convergent supervisory approach across the EU. The guidelines are based on Articles 41, 44, 45 and 246 of the Solvency II Directive. (Final_EN_ORSA_Clean.pdf, pp. 1–2)

The ORSA should strengthen the undertaking’s management and must not be treated merely as a compliance exercise. The undertaking—and particularly its administrative, management or supervisory body—should understand its risks and the capital needs arising from them. The principle of proportionality applies: the ORSA should not become more complex than the calculation of the SCR for small and medium-sized undertakings with non-complex risk profiles. Permitted simplifications for Pillar 1 quantitative requirements may also be used in the ORSA where the relevant conditions are met. (0ae6b432-4ca1-415c-8613-45407266f00b_en.pdf, p. 6)

For groups seeking authorization to produce a **single ORSA document**, they must provide the group supervisor with relevant information explaining how the individual assessments of the included entities are covered and addressed, and how the respective AMSBs are involved through to production of the single ORSA document. (0ae6b432-4ca1-415c-8613-45407266f00b_en.pdf, p. 6; p. 7)

column2: Solvency II guidelines
column3:
The Solvency II guidelines are being revised to make them shorter and limited to what is necessary for a sound and consistent application of Solvency II. The current Guidelines on the valuation of technical provisions were issued in 2015; the 2022 revision concerned best-estimate valuation and applied from 2023. The current revision focuses on the risk-margin calculation for technical provisions, particularly Guidelines 50, 61, 62 and 63 and Technical Annexes IV and VI. It incorporates the Solvency II review’s new exponential, time-dependent “lambda factor,” intended to reflect the time dependency of risks, reduce the risk margin—especially for long-term liabilities—and reduce its sensitivity to interest-rate changes. Guideline 62 and Technical Annex IV were amended, while Guideline 61 and Technical Annex VI were deleted. (Report on revised GLs on valuation of TPs.pdf, p.4)

The revised Guidelines on group solvency specify and harmonise requirements for calculating group solvency. They apply to all group-solvency calculation methods unless otherwise stated, with the standard formula or internal model specified where relevant, and address EEA groups in the context of Articles 215 to 217 of Directive 2009/138/EC (Solvency II Directive). They are addressed to supervisory authorities under Solvency II and apply from 30 January 2027, repealing and replacing the Guidelines on group solvency (EIOPA-BoS-14/181). (dda6cfcc-e3f0-4d40-91a4-b870dfb15522_en.pdf, pp.4–5, 13)

column2: What are the AMLA's 2026 priorities?
column3:
AMLA’s 2026 priorities are to:

- **Complete the Single Rulebook** by delivering core regulatory mandates, including six priority private-sector instruments (RTS, ITS or guidelines), with an emphasis on customer due diligence, business relationships and consistent implementation of AML/CFT obligations. (AMLA sets strategic priorities with 2026-28 Single Programming Document.pdf, p.1-2; AMLA SPD 2026-2028.pdf, p.32)
- **Advance supervisory convergence**, including through direct supervision and by laying the foundations for indirect supervision and oversight. (AMLA sets strategic priorities with 2026-28 Single Programming Document.pdf, p.1-2)
- **Strengthen cooperation among Financial Intelligence Units (FIUs)** by operationalising the FIU framework. (AMLA sets strategic priorities with 2026-28 Single Programming Document.pdf, p.1-2)
- **Develop AMLA’s risk frameworks** to support its supervisory and other functions. (AMLA sets strategic priorities with 2026-28 Single Programming Document.pdf, p.1-2)

Alongside these substantive priorities, AMLA plans to scale its workforce, IT infrastructure and organisational structures. Its digital priorities for 2026–2028 include developing advanced digital solutions, taking over and modernising critical systems, and becoming a leader in data analytics and innovation, while integrating AI systematically across its operations. (A&O Shearman _ FinReg _ AMLA's first single programming document for 2026-2028.pdf, p.1)

column2: AMLA RTS
column3:
AMLA is developing draft Regulatory Technical Standards (RTS) covering, among other matters, proportionate and risk-based customer due diligence (CDD) measures. These RTS aim to harmonise the application of AML/CFT requirements across the Union, apply to obliged entities in both the financial and non-financial sectors, promote simplification, and allow entities to select effective and proportionate measures based on their risks. The consultation paper concerns draft RTS under Article 28(1) of Regulation (EU) 2024/1624 and was published for a three-month consultation period. (3d430294-5171-455c-b565-a86fc5f3cb1c_en.pdf, p.4-5)

AMLA is also preparing draft RTS on cooperation between home and host supervisors. These standards establish a baseline framework for supervisory cooperation concerning cross-border groups of obliged entities, clarify the respective duties of home and host supervisors, and provide practical arrangements—such as communication channels—for day-to-day cooperation and information sharing. The stated legal basis is Article 46(4) of AMLD. Information received from third-country counterparts remains subject to prior consent requirements. (Press Release - Draft RTS on Home-Host Supervisory Cooperation.pdf, p.4-5)

column2: AMLA Single Programming Document
column3:
AMLA’s first Single Programming Document (SPD) covers 2026–2028. It is a multi-year strategic planning document setting out the Authority’s objectives, planned activities, required resources, work programme and strategic priorities as AMLA moves toward full operational capacity. (SPD-2026-2028-Explainer.pdf, p.1; A&O Shearman _ FinReg _ AMLA's first single programming document for 2026-2028.pdf, p.1)

For 2026, the SPD identifies five interlinked workstreams: delivering core regulatory mandates; advancing direct supervision; operationalising the Financial Intelligence Unit (FIU) framework; laying the foundations for indirect supervision and oversight; and developing AMLA’s risk frameworks. AMLA plans to deliver 24 of its 40 mandates in 2026, prioritising effective implementation, simplification, industry-relevant measures and mandates needed for its supervisory and FIU responsibilities. (SPD-2026-2028-Explainer.pdf, p.1) The SPD also includes a 2026–2028 digital roadmap focused on advanced digital solutions, modernising mission-critical systems, and data analytics and innovation, with AI to be systematically integrated into AMLA’s operations. (A&O Shearman _ FinReg _ AMLA's first single programming document for 2026-2028.pdf, p.1) By 2028, AMLA is expected to directly supervise the Union’s financial institutions with the largest geographical footprint and highest risk profile, alongside indirect oversight and FIU coordination. (AMLA SPD 2026-2028.pdf, p.5)

column2: AMLA cross-border FIU cooperation
column3:
AMLA is strengthening cross-border cooperation between EU Financial Intelligence Units (FIUs) by establishing a recurring cycle of joint analyses covering cross-border typologies and emerging risks, including crypto-assets and novel payment channels. Priority cases are intended to be selected transparently and consistently, with analytical outputs routed in a structured way to national authorities and, where relevant, the EPPO, OLAF, Europol and Eurojust. In 2026, AMLA’s team of 27 FIU delegates is expected to be complete, supporting enhanced coordination, information exchange and analytical cooperation. (AMLA SPD 2026-2028.pdf, pp. 23–24)

AMLA is also developing harmonised standards for FIU cooperation, including the standard format for FIU-to-FIU exchanges and regulatory technical standards setting criteria for the cross-border relevance of suspicious transaction reports (STRs). Its consultation proposes objective, structured criteria that can be applied automatically through FIU.net to distinguish between a full cross-border report and a focused “cross-border dissemination,” aiming to make exchanges faster and more consistent while reducing over- and under-sharing. (AMLA SPD 2026-2028.pdf, pp. 23–24; Press Release - AMLA consults on clear rules for cross-border FIU information exchanges.pdf, p. 1)

AMLA will host, maintain and further develop FIU.net, pursue interoperability with national systems, and establish support mechanisms including a helpdesk, training, knowledge-sharing, peer reviews and mediation procedures. Formal working arrangements with Europol, Eurojust, OLAF and the EPPO are also planned. (AMLA SPD 2026-2028.pdf, p. 24)

column2: Do we have an example of a Compliance Monitoring Plan, including the associated risk assessment, for a crypto-asset service provider (CASP) in Luxembourg?
column3:
No. The excerpts do not provide an example or template of a Compliance Monitoring Plan for a Luxembourg crypto-asset service provider, nor do they include an associated enterprise-wide or compliance risk assessment. They also contain no Luxembourg-specific requirements or document.

They do, however, identify matters that could be included in such a plan, including:

- Regular monitoring of suitability assessments and whether staff consider all relevant suitability requirements. (ESMA35-24871704-2922 Guidelines for the criteria on the assessment of knowledge and competence under the Markets in Crypto Assets Regulation, p.17–18)
- Monitoring whether staff can properly assess clients’ objectives, financial situation, knowledge and experience, and explain the risks and rewards of crypto-assets or strategies. (ESMA35-24871704-2922 Guidelines for the criteria on the assessment of knowledge and competence under the Markets in Crypto Assets Regulation, p.17–18)
- Training and monitoring concerning conflicts of interest and inducements. (ESMA35-24871704-2922 Guidelines for the criteria on the assessment of knowledge and competence under the Markets in Crypto Assets Regulation, p.17–18)
- Controls over suitability questionnaires and risk-profiling tools, including coherence checks and mitigation of risks arising from their use. (ESMA35-1872330276-2031_Guidelines_on_suitability_and_periodic_statement_MiCA.pdf, p.20)

Thus, the excerpts can support the content of a Compliance Monitoring Plan, but they do not contain the requested completed example or risk assessment.

column2: In the context of a Long Form Report (external audit) of a payment institution, do we have a model approach for the review of the AML/CFT framework?
column3:
No specific Long Form Report (external audit) template or detailed AML/CFT audit programme is provided in the excerpts. They do, however, support a **risk-based review approach**, rather than a purely checklist-based review. The review should consider the payment institution’s inherent financial-crime risks, whether its controls effectively mitigate those risks, and whether the supervisory or audit effort is proportionate to its ML/TF risk profile. Particular attention should be given to cross-border activities, agent networks and the use of agents, and products, delivery channels or technologies whose financial-crime risks may not have been adequately identified at design or implementation stage (Recommendations for Regulating and Supervising Bank and Non-bank Payment Service Providers Offering Cross-border Payment Services_ Final report.pdf, pp.23–24).

A practical review structure can also document: (i) the reasons for any non-compliance; (ii) whether the issue is confirmed and constitutes a regulatory breach; (iii) any mitigating factors; and (iv) the appropriate response or remediation. The framework should further be assessed through governance, risk management and operational-risk considerations, with controls rated, for example, as strong or adequate based on the quality of management, organisation and controls and their compatibility with the institution’s nature and complexity (Supervisory methodology 2025.pdf, pp.11–12). Accordingly, the excerpts provide principles for developing a Long Form Report methodology, but not a prescribed model report or specific legal basis.

column2: Do we have examples of valuation policy and risk management policy for an ISA with infrastructure funds?
column3:
Yes. The excerpts provide useful examples, although they do not contain a complete, ISA-specific policy template for infrastructure funds.

For **valuation policy**, the scope can cover infrastructure-related immovable assets and project finance, including onshore and offshore solar or wind projects, hydropower facilities, toll roads, railways and similar infrastructure. Good practice is to document the assets and sub-types covered across entities, business lines and portfolios; specify the valuation methods used; and incorporate relevant climate and nature risk drivers, including the effect of insurance. (Good practices for climate and nature risk management.pdf, pp.121–122) Valuation governance can also include controls over the accuracy of investment information, the proportion of assets valued using alternative methods, and back-testing or analysis of valuation changes. (d1ef2dd1-043d-4c0c-8e49-498cbcf8973c_en.pdf, p.28)

For **risk management policy**, the excerpts identify policies and procedures covering credit assessment, pricing and granting, credit monitoring, renewal and refinancing, collateral management, concentration risk, operational risk, borrower assessment and scoring, valuation and impairment, problem debt and staff expertise. They also mention leverage and diversification limits and restrictions on certain activities, such as non-hedging derivatives, short selling and securities lending. (EUR-Lex - 52021SC0340 - EN - EUR-Lex.pdf, pp.100–101) For infrastructure exposures, the policy should additionally address risk-transfer and hedging arrangements, including governance, effectiveness, basis risk, complexity, stress-test results, asset-liability management, counterparty or reinsurer credit risk and climate-related catastrophe risks. (d1ef2dd1-043d-4c0c-8e49-498cbcf8973c_en.pdf, p.28)

The excerpts do not name a specific legal basis or provide a complete policy expressly labelled for an “ISA with infrastructure funds.”

column2: Do we have a due diligence questionnaire to send to UCITS fund distributors?
column3:
Yes. The excerpts indicate that a **distribution due diligence questionnaire** is used for distributor oversight. It is generally a process of asking questions, receiving and assessing the distributor’s answers, to verify compliance with applicable marketing laws and regulations, contractual requirements, and AML/CTF obligations. The objective is to ensure that the distributor complies with marketing and governance rules and AML/CTF requirements when marketing the fund. (Delegate Due Diligence.pdf, p.5–6)

column2: What are the regulatory obligations of an MFI for FATCA/CRS reporting, and do we have an example of an internal FATCA/CRS policy?
column3:
An MFI acting as a reporting Financial Institution must comply with both FATCA and CRS reporting obligations to the Luxembourg tax authorities. For fiscal year 2025, reporting is due by **30 June 2026**; where applicable, it may submit a “zero” or “nil” report if it has no reportable accounts. For FATCA, a Foreign Financial Institution should generally register and obtain a **Global Intermediary Identification Number (GIIN)**, whereas no CRS registration is required. FATCA exemptions may apply to certain entities or accounts, while CRS exemptions are more limited. (FATCA & CRS _ Obligations for Reporting Financial Institutions for year 2025, pp. 1–2)

The MFI must establish and evidence appropriate due-diligence and compliance processes, monitor any third-party service providers, retain evidence of their work and of the controls performed, and keep copies of all reports—including initial filings, additions, cancellations and corrections—together with Luxembourg tax administration validation feedback. Under Article 2(1) of the Luxembourg CRS Law, relevant documentation must be retained for **10 years**, including client files, financial-position valuations, the Register of Actions, written procedures and policies, submitted reports, validation feedback and other evidence of compliance; records must be readily available for audit. (Updated Luxembourg CRS FAQ reinforce importance of compliance records, pp. 3–4) Non-compliance may result in a EUR 10,000 penalty for no reporting, up to EUR 250,000 for breaches such as failures in due diligence or compliance setup, and the main penalty plus 0.5% of amounts that should have been reported for incomplete, late or inaccurate reporting. (FATCA & CRS _ Obligations for Reporting Financial Institutions for year 2025, p. 1)

The excerpts confirm that the MFI should maintain written FATCA/CRS procedures and policies, but **they do not provide an example of an internal FATCA/CRS policy**. (Updated Luxembourg CRS FAQ reinforce importance of compliance records, p. 3)

column2: What are the supervisory obligations of an MFI when functions are delegated directly by the fund's general partner rather than by the MFI itself?
column3:
The excerpts do not expressly address a situation in which the fund’s general partner delegates functions directly, rather than the MFI/AIFM delegating them. However, they establish that the AIFM remains fully responsible and liable to investors for the provision of the fund-management functions. Delegation therefore does not remove the AIFM’s supervisory responsibility or liability merely because the delegation is arranged through another party. (EUR-Lex - 52021SC0340 - EN - EUR-Lex.pdf, p.150–151)

Accordingly, the AIFM should maintain effective oversight and information flows with any third party involved, ensure adequate internal controls, and ensure that its governing body and senior management remain responsible for compliance with the AIFM’s obligations. Where the arrangement is treated as delegation of core functions, the delegate must meet the stated authorisation, competence, resources and reputation requirements; the AIFM must supervise the delegate, be able to withdraw the delegation immediately, and ensure that the competent authorities are notified before the arrangement becomes effective. (esma34-45-688_final_report_on_integrating_sustainability_risks_and_factors_in_the_ucits_directive_and_the_aifmd.pdf, p.15–16; EUR-Lex - 52021SC0340 - EN - EUR-Lex.pdf, p.150–151)

column2: Investor blocked account monitoring system (the function of transfer agent/TA is outsourced). Apart from sending reminders to the TA to obtain the missing documentation to complete/finalize the KYC, what more can IFM do? Make a declaration of suspicion, escalate the subject to the Board?
column3:
Beyond reminders, the IFM should treat the matter as a documented AML/KYC case rather than merely an administrative follow-up. It should review the investor’s KYC information, transaction history and risk profile; determine whether a temporary investigative restriction or manual-review status is appropriate; and ensure that the account-level restriction, its date, rationale, supporting evidence and follow-up actions are recorded. The investor may be informed, within legal limits, of the restriction and of the documentation or explanations required. (What Is a Blocked Account in Anti‑Money Laundering_.pdf, p.4; What Is a Blocked Account in Anti‑Money Laundering_.pdf, p.6-7)

Because the TA is outsourced, the IFM should use its outsourcing-governance framework: perform risk-based due diligence, obtain periodic certifications or assessments where appropriate, address findings through the relevant oversight team, and monitor the TA through periodic service reviews. For critical providers such as TAs, the excerpt indicates that annual onsite due diligence is expected. (Delegate Due Diligence.pdf, p.6)

A declaration of suspicion should be considered where the review identifies suspected money laundering or terrorist financing; the excerpt describes filing a SAR or equivalent report with the FIU as part of the workflow. A sanctions-related match requires the applicable blocking action and notification to the competent authority. Mere failure to provide documents, without indicators of ML/TF or sanctions exposure, is not identified in the excerpts as sufficient by itself to justify a suspicion report. (What Is a Blocked Account in Anti‑Money Laundering_.pdf, p.4) Escalation to the IFM’s internal oversight function is appropriate, particularly for material or unresolved TA deficiencies; escalation specifically to the Board is not addressed in the excerpts and should therefore depend on the IFM’s internal governance and escalation thresholds. (Delegate Due Diligence.pdf, p.6)

column2: What obligations are imposed on an AIFM investing in illiquid securities under the Market Abuse Regulation (MAD 2)?
column3:
The excerpts do **not identify any specific obligation imposed by MAD 2** on an AIFM investing in illiquid securities. They refer instead to AIFMD/AIFM-related supervisory and liquidity obligations.

Relevant obligations described are:

- The AIFM must report information to its national competent authority, including the main instruments traded by the AIFs it manages, principal exposures and significant investment concentrations. A full-scope AIFM must also report investment strategies, principal markets, investor concentration, risk profiles—including liquidity risk—and stress-test results. The home-state authority must make the information available to other relevant authorities, ESMA and the ESRB. (52021SC0340, pp.144–145)
- The AIFM must implement liquidity-risk limits that take account of each AIF’s investment strategy and assets and are consistent with the risk profile disclosed to investors. The investment strategy, liquidity profile and redemption policy must allow redemptions consistently with the fair treatment of all investors and the AIF’s redemption obligations. (FR13_22 Thematic Review on Liquidity Risk Management Recommendations, p.18)
- Where anti-dilution levies are used, they should reflect the estimated explicit and implicit portfolio-transaction costs caused by subscriptions or redemptions, including significant market impact from buying or selling assets to meet those transactions. (ESMA34-1985693317-1259_Final_Report_on_the_Draft_Regulatory_Technical_Standards_on_Liquidity_Management_Tools_under_the_AIFMD_and_UCITS_Directive, p.47)

Thus, based on these excerpts, no MAD 2-specific illiquid-securities requirement can be stated; the documented requirements concern supervisory reporting, liquidity-risk limits and fair handling of investor subscriptions and redemptions.

column2: Do we have performance assessment frameworks that incorporate sustainability objectives (ESG) for a credit institution?
column3:
Yes. The excerpts support an ESG-integrated performance and risk-assessment framework for a credit institution. Institutions are expected to identify and measure ESG risks using multiple methodologies, integrate them into the regular risk-management framework, risk appetite, internal controls and ICAAP, and monitor them through internal reporting, including backward- and forward-looking ESG risk metrics and indicators. (Final Guidelines on the management of ESG risks.pdf, p.3; Circular 26_905.pdf, p.6)

The framework also incorporates forward-looking sustainability objectives through strategies, policies and transition planning over short-, medium- and long-term horizons, including at least 10 years. Institutions should promote awareness of their ESG strategic objectives and commitments, and the first line of defence should assess ESG risks during client onboarding, credit applications, credit reviews and ongoing monitoring. (Circular 26_905.pdf, pp.6, 33) The excerpts do not, however, specify a standalone ESG employee-performance appraisal or remuneration framework; they describe an ESG-integrated risk, strategy, monitoring and credit-assessment framework.

column2: Quelles sont les travaux que le réviseur d'entreprises doit effectuer dans le cas d'une erreur de calcul de NAV selon la circulaire CSSF 24/856 (par type d'erreur) ?
column3:
Selon la circulaire CSSF 24/856, les travaux du réviseur d’entreprises (REA) diffèrent selon la nature de l’erreur :

- **Non-respect actif des règles d’investissement de l’OPC** : le réviseur doit calculer les gains ou pertes subis par l’OPC du fait de la correction, déterminer les montants à verser à titre d’indemnisation, vérifier que la méthode de calcul de l’impact est cohérente avec la circulaire et les procédures internes applicables, vérifier le paiement effectif de l’indemnisation à l’OPC et déterminer si le non-respect a entraîné une erreur significative de calcul de la VNI. Il doit également effectuer, par sondage, des contrôles sur la classification correcte des cas de non-respect « passif ». (CSSF24_856eng.pdf, p.40-41)

- **Toute autre erreur, notamment une erreur de calcul de la VNI** : le réviseur doit, sur la base des impacts identifiés, déterminer les montants à indemniser à l’OPC et/ou aux investisseurs, vérifier que la méthode de calcul des gains et/ou pertes est appropriée au type d’erreur, puis vérifier le paiement effectif de l’indemnisation conformément à la section 7.2. (CSSF24_856eng.pdf, p.40-41)

Pour une **erreur significative de calcul de la VNI**, les VNI erronées doivent être corrigées sans délai et le préjudice doit être chiffré sur la base des VNI corrigées. L’impact doit notamment distinguer les investisseurs ayant été remboursés pendant la période d’erreur et ceux ayant souscrit pendant cette période sur la base d’une VNI erronée. (cssf24_856.pdf, p.20-21)

column2: Quels sont les changements de principes comptables dans les états financiers en cas de liquidation ?
column3:
Dans le projet de révision de l’OIC 5, la disparition de la présomption de continuité d’exploitation modifie la logique d’évaluation : les actifs et passifs ne sont plus appréciés selon leur contribution à la génération de produits, mais selon leur réalisation ou leur extinction dans le cadre de la liquidation. Pour les sociétés sans poursuite d’activité, les actifs corporels et incorporels, les participations et les titres de créance sont évalués au plus bas entre leur valeur comptable au début de la liquidation et leur valeur de réalisation présumée déduite des tendances du marché. Les actifs corporels et incorporels ne sont plus amortis, et les titres de créance ne sont plus évalués au coût amorti. Les créances sont comptabilisées à leur valeur présumée de réalisation et les passifs à leur valeur présumée d’extinction ; le coût amorti et l’actualisation ne s’appliquent pas, sauf éléments certains affectant la valeur d’extinction, tels que pénalités ou escomptes. (OIC 5_ key operational changes - LEXIA.pdf, p.1)

Les charges de liquidation font également l’objet d’une approche plus prudente : des provisions ne sont constituées que pour les charges correspondant à une obligation inévitable de la société et qui ne sont pas nécessaires à l’achèvement de la liquidation. Les prévisions relatives à l’issue de la procédure ne sont plus intégrées dans une estimation prospective globale, mais présentées dans l’annexe, avec l’évolution attendue des encaissements et des paiements et l’appréciation de leur suffisance pour régler intégralement les obligations de la liquidation. (2024-04-09-Bozza-per-consultazione-Principio-contabile-OIC-5-Bilanci-di-Liquidazione-1.pdf, p.38-39)

Enfin, la distinction entre actif circulant et actif immobilisé perd sa pertinence en liquidation. Lorsqu’aucune poursuite d’activité, même provisoire ou limitée à certaines branches, n’est prévue, le projet impose des modèles spécifiques de bilan et de compte de résultat ainsi qu’un tableau des flux de trésorerie dédié. (2024-04-09-Bozza-per-consultazione-Principio-contabile-OIC-5-Bilanci-di-Liquidazione-1.pdf, p.38-39 ; OIC 5_ key operational changes - LEXIA.pdf, p.1)

column2: Quels sont les impacts de la nouvelle norme IFRS 18 ?
column3:
La norme IFRS 18 modifie principalement la **présentation et les informations à fournir**, sans être censée modifier la manière dont les entreprises mesurent leur performance financière. Elle introduit cinq catégories de classement des produits et charges — **exploitation, investissement, financement, impôts sur le résultat et activités abandonnées** — ainsi que deux sous-totaux obligatoires : le **résultat opérationnel** et le **résultat avant financement et impôts sur le résultat**. Elle renforce également les règles d’agrégation, de désagrégation et de libellé des postes, afin d’améliorer la lisibilité et la comparabilité des états financiers. ( *IFRS 18_ what the new standard means for your financial reporting*, p. 2-3 ; *IFRS 18_ Introduction for Insurers*, p. 4-5)

Les entreprises devront aussi fournir des informations auditées sur les **mesures de performance définies par la direction** (« Management-Defined Performance Measures », MPM). La transition aura des conséquences pratiques importantes pour les équipes financières : analyse des impacts et des reclassements, correspondance entre les plans comptables et les nouvelles catégories IFRS 18, adaptation des ERP et des structures de gestion de la performance, renforcement des contrôles et évolution des communications internes et externes. Les principaux ratios financiers peuvent également être affectés, car leur calcul peut varier selon la présentation retenue sous IFRS 18 ; l’effet dépendra notamment du ratio et du profil de l’utilisateur des états financiers. ( *IFRS 18_ what the new standard means for your financial reporting*, p. 2-3 ; *IFRS 18 Presentation and Disclosure in Financial Statements - CBS Research Portal*, p. 1-2 ; *IFRS 18_ Introduction for Insurers*, p. 4-5)

column2: What are the ICT governance requirements for Luxembourg-supervised entities?
column3:
Luxembourg-supervised financial entities within the scope of DORA must implement governance arrangements for ICT third-party services. DORA has applied to CSSF-supervised financial entities in scope since 17 January 2025. Circular CSSF 25/882 provides practical instructions for submitting information and reporting on ICT third-party providers, and recalls general requirements for the use of third-party ICT services, taking account of Luxembourg national financial-services laws. (cssf25_882eng.pdf, pp. 1–2)

ICT governance must be designed in the context of the entity’s business model as a whole, with due regard to activities regulated under the LFS, the LPS, or other national laws granting supervisory competence to the CSSF. This applies in particular when entities perform ICT outsourcing, and the circular also covers specified Luxembourg entities such as Article 125-1 UCITS management companies and Luxembourg branches of certain third-country institutions. (Circular CSSF 22_806.pdf, p. 10) Governance arrangements must be proportionate to factors including the volume and complexity of operations, the entity’s size, staffing, group structure, outsourcing and ICT concentration risks, and the architecture and continuity of IT systems. The proportionality assessment must be documented in writing and approved by the supervisory body at least annually. (cssf26_906eng.pdf, pp. 6–7) For institutions covered by the relevant requirements, arrangements must also support full compliance with the applicable governance and risk-management provisions, and central administration—including the decision-making and administrative centres—must be located in Luxembourg, rather than having only a Luxembourg registered office. (cssf26_906eng.pdf, p. 7)

column2: What are the ECB's supervisory priorities?
column3:
The ECB’s supervisory priorities for 2026–2028 are to:

- **Strengthen banks’ resilience to geopolitical risks and macro-financial uncertainties**, including geopolitical tensions, trade fragmentation, climate- and nature-related risks, demographic change and rapid technological transformation. (Supervisory Priorities for 2026 - 2028 _ Management Solutions.pdf, p.1)
- **Strengthen operational resilience and ICT capabilities**, including the management of operational, IT-outsourcing and cybersecurity risks. (Supervisory Priorities for 2026 - 2028 _ Management Solutions.pdf, p.1; ECB Banking Supervision_ SSM supervisory priorities for 2024-2026.pdf, p.3)
- **Advance digital transformation**, with robust digital and particularly AI-related strategies supported by appropriate governance and risk-management frameworks. (Supervisory Priorities 2026-28.pdf, pp.2–3)

The ECB will address these priorities through targeted supervisory work programmes, while continuing regular supervision, follow-up work on past priorities and proportionate application of the priorities to less significant institutions. (Supervisory Priorities 2026-28.pdf, pp.2–3)

column2: What are the draft RTS on Customer Due Diligence?
column3:
The draft Regulatory Technical Standards (RTS) on Customer Due Diligence (CDD) set out requirements for, and information to be collected during, simplified, standard and enhanced due diligence. They also specify: the types of simplified due diligence measures permitted; risk factors linked to features of electronic money; reliable and independent information sources for verifying identification data; and the attributes that electronic identification methods and qualified trust services must have to meet identification and verification requirements. The RTS are intended to ensure a high level of harmonisation while preserving a risk-based and proportionate approach. *(AMLA Public Hearing - Draft RTS under Article 28(1) AMLR.pdf, pp. 9–11)*

Compared with the earlier EBA draft, the revised draft includes a new recital addressing powers of representation and provisions on the information obliged entities must collect to verify the existence and scope of a representative’s authority. Article 16 of the draft RTS covers identification and verification of a person claiming to act on behalf of a customer, while Article 22 AMLR covers identification and verification of customers and beneficial owners. *(2026 AML_CFT Consultations - Unpacking AMLA's New Draft RTS_ Key Takeaways for the Financial and Non‑Financial Sectors_br__ _ Herbert Smith Freehills Kramer _ Global law firm.pdf, pp. 1–2, 4)* The framework also applies a risk-based frequency for updating customer information: no more than one year for higher-risk customers and no more than five years for other customers. *(2026 AML_CFT Consultations - Unpacking AMLA's New Draft RTS_ Key Takeaways for the Financial and Non‑Financial Sectors_br__ _ Herbert Smith Freehills Kramer _ Global law firm.pdf, p. 4)*

column2: What are the key provisions of Delegated Regulation (EU) 2017/565?
column3:
Commission Delegated Regulation (EU) 2017/565 supplements Directive 2014/65/EU by setting detailed **organisational requirements and operating conditions for investment firms**, and by defining terms used for that Directive. It forms part of the EU regulatory framework for investment services and activities, including ancillary services where relevant. The framework also covers organisational requirements for investment firms, regulated markets and data-reporting services providers, as well as transaction-reporting requirements for financial instruments. (Delegated regulation - 2017_565 - EN - EUR-Lex.pdf, pp.1, 5)

The key organisational areas identified in the MiFID II framework include **general organisational requirements, risk management and conflicts of interest**. The related product-governance framework covers manufacturers’ and distributors’ duties to define and review the target market. Subsequent proposed amendments also addressed the integration of sustainability risks, ESG considerations and ESG preferences into relevant MiFID II provisions. (esma35-43-1737_final_report_on_integrating_sustainability_risks_and_factors_in_the_mifid_ii.pdf, pp.24–25) The Regulation entered into force following its publication and applied from 3 January 2018; the EUR-Lex record indicates that it has since been amended and that the consolidated version was current as of 2 August 2022. (Delegated regulation - 2017_565 - EN - EUR-Lex.pdf, p.1)

column2: What are the ESMA guidelines on suitability?
column3:
ESMA’s suitability guidelines aim to improve clarity and promote convergence in how suitability requirements are implemented. Under the MiFID suitability framework, when an investment firm provides investment advice or portfolio management, it must ensure that each transaction recommended—or entered into for portfolio management—is suitable for the particular client or prospective client. The suitability guidance is divided into general and supporting guidelines and addresses only certain aspects of MiFID. (cssf07_307eng.pdf, pp.100–101)

For crypto-assets, ESMA’s guidelines apply to the suitability requirements under Article 81 of MiCA and to the format of periodic statements for crypto-asset portfolio management. A “suitability assessment” is the complete process of collecting client information and assessing whether a crypto-asset is suitable, based on the crypto-asset service provider’s sound understanding of the crypto-assets it may recommend or invest in for the client. These guidelines apply 60 calendar days after publication on ESMA’s website in all official EU languages. (ESMA35-1872330276-2031_Guidelines_on_suitability_and_periodic_statement_MiCA.pdf, pp.5–6)

The guidelines are addressed to competent authorities under ESMA’s “comply or explain” framework and also to financial-market participants, although participants are not required to report whether they comply with the guidelines. (cssf07_307eng.pdf, p.100)

column2: What is ESMA's supervisory briefing on outsourcing?
column3:
ESMA’s outsourcing supervisory guidance in the excerpts is the **Guidelines on Outsourcing to Cloud Service Providers**. They are intended to help firms and competent authorities identify, address and monitor risks throughout the cloud-outsourcing lifecycle: deciding whether to outsource, selecting a cloud service provider, overseeing the outsourced activities, and establishing exit strategies. (ESMA65-294529287-4737_Guidelines_on_outsourcing_to_cloud_service_providers.pdf, p.7)

The guidelines expect competent authorities and firms to make every effort to comply. Competent authorities should incorporate them into their national legal or supervisory frameworks where appropriate and use supervision to ensure that firms comply. They must notify ESMA within two months of publication in all EU official languages whether they comply, intend to comply, or do not intend to comply; where they do not comply, they must also provide reasons. Firms themselves are not required to report their compliance status to ESMA. (ESMA65-294529287-4737_Guidelines_on_outsourcing_to_cloud_service_providers.pdf, pp.7–8)

column2: What are the current consultation proposals for the AIFMD review?
column3:
The excerpts indicate that the AIFMD review is pursuing **targeted improvements**, rather than a wholesale redesign, because the framework has generally achieved its objectives. The main identified proposal area is to improve the **quality, completeness and detail of data reported to supervisors**, so that financial-stability risks and their potential spillovers can be monitored and managed more effectively. (52021SC0340, p.13–14)

The review also considers developments requiring further policy work, including **loan-originating funds, liquidity-management tools, delegation by fund managers and improved reporting data**. In addition, proposals concerning the treatment of **central securities depositories (CSDs) as delegates of depositaries** under the AIFMD should be extended to the UCITS framework. (52021SC0340, p.95–96; 52021SC0340, p.13–14) The excerpts describe the consultation as seeking stakeholder views on achieving a more effective and efficient EU AIF market; they do not set out a complete list of final legislative proposals. (52021SC0340, p.140–141)

column2: What are the requirements for a merger under the Luxembourg law on securitisation?
column3:
The excerpts indicate that a Luxembourg securitisation company may merge under the **simplified merger procedure referred to in Articles 278 to 280 of the Company Law**. The merger is documented through formal “Terms of Merger” or a merger proposal approved by the companies’ boards of directors. (C-N° 1938 _ 31 juillet 2015.pdf, pp.2–4)

The merger may involve the transfer to the absorbing company of **all assets, liabilities, rights, obligations and contracts**, without exception or reservation. The merger proposal must be published, and the documents required by **Article 267 of the 1915 Law** must be deposited at the registered office of the merging company **one month before the general meetings**; the relevant reports are to be annexed to the deed. The shareholders must then approve the merger proposal. (C-N° 59 _ 12 janvier 2009.pdf, p.29) The excerpts do not set out additional requirements specific to securitisation companies beyond these merger formalities.

column2: How does ESMA's Q&A on MiFID II treat best execution?
column3:
The Q&A presents best execution as a broad, overarching obligation. Investment firms must take **all reasonable steps to obtain the best possible result for clients**, considering price, costs, speed, likelihood of execution and settlement, order size, nature, and any other consideration relevant to execution. The requirement applies to firms executing orders or decisions to deal, including firms transmitting or placing orders with other entities for execution. It sets a high-level standard and gives firms considerable flexibility, while still requiring compliance with specific provisions. (cssf07_307eng.pdf, p.59)

The Q&A identifies the relevant provisions as Article 21 of Level 1, Articles 44 and 46 of Level 2, and, indirectly for portfolio-management decisions, Article 45(7). It expressly does **not** address the scope of best execution under MiFID or how it applies in dealer markets. The Commission’s response is appended to the Q&A but is not part of the Q&A itself; CESR nevertheless considered that the response provided a sufficient basis for implementation and that no further work was needed at that time, while leaving open the possibility of reviewing application of the requirements in future. (cssf07_307eng.pdf, p.58-59)

column2: what are the customer due diligence requirements under the AMLR?
column3:
Under the AMLR, customer due diligence (CDD) is to be harmonised through AMLA standards covering **standard, simplified and enhanced due diligence**. Obliged entities must collect the minimum information specified for each type of CDD, with simplified measures tailored to lower-risk sectors, products and situations. The requirements also cover the risk factors for exemptions relating to low-value electronic-money instruments. (AMLA Level 2 Package_ 23 RTS, ITS and Guidelines Due July 10, 2026 _ financialregulations.eu.pdf, pp. 2–3; Consultation-Paper-on-Response-to-Call-for-Advice-new-AMLA-mandates.pdf, p. 11)

CDD must include the **identification and verification of customers and beneficial owners**, as well as identification and verification of anyone purporting to act on behalf of the customer. Verification may use reliable and independent information sources; remote verification may use electronic identification means meeting the applicable “substantial” or “high” assurance levels under Regulation (EU) 910/2014 and relevant qualified trust services. The RTS will also specify the attributes that electronic identification means and qualified trust services must have for CDD purposes. (2026 AML_CFT Consultations - Unpacking AMLA's New Draft RTS_ Key Takeaways for the Financial and Non‑Financial Sectors_br__ _ Herbert Smith Freehills Kramer _ Global law firm.pdf, p. 4; Consultation-Paper-on-Response-to-Call-for-Advice-new-AMLA-mandates.pdf, p. 11)

Customer information and documents must be kept up to date on a risk-sensitive basis: for higher-risk customers, the interval between updates must not exceed one year; for other customers, it must not exceed five years. The harmonised CDD requirements establish an EU minimum, while competent authorities or AMLA may impose additional requirements for particular risk categories. (2026 AML_CFT Consultations - Unpacking AMLA's New Draft RTS_ Key Takeaways for the Financial and Non‑Financial Sectors_br__ _ Herbert Smith Freehills Kramer _ Global law firm.pdf, p. 4; AMLA Level 2 Package_ 23 RTS, ITS and Guidelines Due July 10, 2026 _ financialregulations.eu.pdf, pp. 2–3)
