column2: what are the triggers for enhanced due diligence (EDD)?
column3:
Enhanced due diligence (EDD) is triggered when the risk associated with a business relationship or occasional transaction increases. This includes relationships or transactions involving **high-risk third countries** and other **high-risk customers or accounts**. A material change in the customer’s profile or other information affecting the risk assessment should also prompt a review and, where appropriate, updated EDD. (EBA GL 2021 02 - consolidated (amended by EBA GL 2023 03)_EN.docx.pdf, pp. 58–59, 79–80)

EDD is also indicated where there are doubts about the legitimate origin of a customer’s funds or wealth, particularly where the risk is particularly high. In addition, accounts that have previously been blocked may require EDD to reassess their risk profile before unblocking. (EBA GL 2021 02 - consolidated (amended by EBA GL 2023 03)_EN.docx.pdf, p. 79; What Is a Blocked Account in Anti‑Money Laundering_.pdf, p. 6)

column2: what is the difference between policy and a procedure under cssf rules?
column3:
Under CSSF rules, a **policy** sets out the framework for implementation: it contains the detailed measures, principles, responsibilities and processes that govern how the institution should operate. For example, an outsourcing policy must define the main lifecycle phases and the relevant principles, responsibilities and processes. (cssf20_758eng.pdf, p.25-26; Circular CSSF 22_806.pdf, p.24)

A **procedure** explains **how the policy is put into practice**. CSSF describes procedures as the work instructions governing implementation. The term is broad and includes the measures, instructions and rules governing the organisation and internal functioning of the institution. (cssf20_758eng.pdf, p.25-26)

In short: **policy = what must be achieved and the governing framework; procedure = the operational instructions for achieving it.**

column2: what would be the frequency of compliance monitoring reviews
column3:
Compliance monitoring reviews should be conducted **regularly, typically at least annually**, through an independent internal or external compliance review. The frequency should be proportionate to the firm’s ML/TF risks and should include checking CDD documentation and the effectiveness of internal controls (RISK-BASED APPROACH GUIDANCE FOR LEGAL PROFESSIONALS.pdf, pp. 53–54).

For IRRBB monitoring, the excerpts do not prescribe a fixed interval: monitoring and reporting should occur at an **appropriate frequency depending on the scale, complexity, and level of exposures**, while internal-audit reviews should be sufficiently frequent to cover the main elements of the framework (Final Report on revised SREP and supervisory stress testing Guidelines.pdf, p. 107).

column2: what are the record-keeping requirement of AML/CFT?
column3:
AML/CFT record-keeping requirements include maintaining records of all necessary domestic and international transactions for at least five years after completion. Transaction records must be detailed enough to reconstruct individual transactions and, where necessary, provide evidence for the prosecution of criminal activity. (FATF Methodology 22 Feb 2013.pdf.coredownload.inline.pdf, p.50)

Firms must also retain CDD information, account files, business correspondence, and the results of analyses for at least five years after the business relationship ends or, for an occasional transaction, after the transaction date. These records must be made available swiftly to domestic competent authorities when properly authorised. (FATF Methodology 22 Feb 2013.pdf.coredownload.inline.pdf, p.50) In addition, firms must keep records of CDD information, their risk assessments, and transactions, and ensure that the records demonstrate to the competent authority that their AML/CFT measures are adequate in light of the ML/TF risk. (EBA GL 2021 02 - consolidated (amended by EBA GL 2023 03)_EN.docx.pdf, p.43)

column2: what are the requirements for staff AML/CFT training?
column3:
Legal professionals must provide staff with AML/CFT training under **R.18**, and firms should implement a **documented programme of ongoing staff AML/CFT awareness and training**. Training should be firm-wide for all relevant personnel and cover, at a minimum, general information on applicable AML/CFT laws, regulations, and the firm’s internal policies. Firms should also maintain staff awareness of suspicious transaction reporting (STR) filing requirements. (RISK-BASED APPROACH GUIDANCE FOR LEGAL PROFESSIONALS.pdf, pp. 53–54)

Training must be risk- and role-based. Staff working with higher-risk clients or higher-risk matters should receive enhanced, targeted training, and content should reflect their AML/CFT responsibilities—for example, false-document training for personnel conducting identification and verification, and red-flag training for those performing client or transaction risk assessments. Training may be delivered in various practical formats, including group study, guidance or policy briefings, email updates, and fact-based or hypothetical case studies. Staff should also understand how AML/CFT requirements interact with legal professional privilege and professional secrecy, including when those protections apply and when they do not. (RISK-BASED APPROACH GUIDANCE FOR LEGAL PROFESSIONALS.pdf, pp. 54–55)

column3:
The compliance charter must define the compliance function’s reporting lines, including the Chief Compliance Officer’s responsibilities and reporting arrangements. It must also describe the function’s relationships with the risk-control and internal-audit functions, including any delegation or coordination arrangements. (cssf26_906eng.pdf, p.34–35; cssf20_758eng.pdf, p.48)

The Chief Compliance Officer must have the right to contact the chairperson of the supervisory body or, where applicable, the relevant specialised committee directly and on their own initiative, as well as the CSSF. Under the terminology used in the earlier excerpt, this means direct access to the chairperson of the Board of Directors, the audit or compliance committee, and the CSSF. column2: what are the requirements for outsourcing critical functions?
column3:
For outsourcing a critical or important operational function, the undertaking must:

- Determine whether the arrangement constitutes outsourcing and, if so, whether the function is critical or important. For critical or important functions, it must conduct a detailed risk assessment of the function and detailed due diligence on the service provider. Cloud outsourcing must be integrated into the undertaking’s overall outsourcing process and governance. (8b80b926-ad14-48fc-9618-325234845d03_en.pdf, p.69)
- Define the roles and responsibilities of the relevant functions, including the AMSB and the ICT, information security, compliance, risk management and internal audit functions. It must also establish approval, implementation, monitoring, management and renewal processes and reporting procedures. (8b80b926-ad14-48fc-9618-325234845d03_en.pdf, pp.15–16)
- Maintain proportionate oversight, including recurring risk assessments and provider due diligence, monitoring and management controls such as verification of the service-level agreement, and appropriate security standards and controls. The arrangement must address the applicable contractual requirements referred to in Guideline 10. (8b80b926-ad14-48fc-9618-325234845d03_en.pdf, pp.15–16)
- Meet documentation requirements and provide written notification to the supervisory authority regarding cloud outsourcing of critical or important operational functions or activities. Each such arrangement must also have a documented and, where appropriate, sufficiently tested exit strategy proportionate to the risks, covering possible discontinuation, reintegration or transfer of the services. (c53462d9-ee1b-4aeb-8706-22852508b7c5_en.pdf, pp.5–6)

More generally, the undertaking should identify, measure, monitor, manage and report risks arising from third-party arrangements, whether or not the provider is a cloud service provider. Less material outsourcing also requires risk assessment and due diligence, but the requirements for critical or important functions are the more detailed ones described above. (8b80b926-ad14-48fc-9618-325234845d03_en.pdf, p.69)

column2: what are the requirements for the internal audit function?
column3:
The internal audit function must be staffed by persons with sufficient knowledge of audit techniques. It must remain independent and objective: internal auditors must not be responsible for preparing or establishing the institution’s central administration or internal governance arrangements, although they may contribute opinions and recommendations on sound internal controls. Conflicts of interest must be avoided, including through rotation of control assignments where possible and by not auditing activities or functions that auditors recently performed themselves. The risk management and compliance functions may not form part of internal audit. (cssf20_758eng.pdf, p.52; cssf26_906eng.pdf, p.42)

The function’s objectives, responsibilities and powers must be set out in an internal audit charter, drafted by internal audit and approved by authorised management, confirmed where appropriate by the audit committee, and ultimately approved by the Board of Directors. The charter must cover the function’s organisational position and key characteristics; its authority to review all institutional activities—including branches, subsidiaries and outsourced activities—and access relevant documents, records and personnel; reporting lines; relationships with compliance and risk control; use of third parties; consulting and special assignments; the head of internal audit’s responsibilities and reporting lines; and the Chief Internal Auditor’s direct right to contact the Board chair, audit committee members where applicable, and the CSSF. (cssf20_758eng.pdf, p.51)

Its scope must include, at a minimum according to the institution’s organisation and the nature, scale and complexity of its activities, assessing compliance with laws, regulations and CSSF prudential requirements; the effectiveness and efficiency of central administration, governance and internal controls, including risk control and compliance; the adequacy of administrative, accounting and IT organisation; safeguarding of values and assets; and segregation of duties and transaction execution. (cssf20_758eng.pdf, p.52) If operational tasks are outsourced, the external provider must work under the institution’s internal audit plan and work programme, document its work in detail, and prepare a report for each mission for submission to the management body, audit committee where applicable, and supervisory body. Where the provider is an approved statutory auditor, it must be independent of the institution’s statutory auditor and approved statutory audit firm. (cssf26_906eng.pdf, p.42–43)

column2: what are the requirements for conflict for interest management?
column3:
The institution must maintain a conflict-of-interest management policy covering all conflicts arising from economic, personal, professional, or political purposes, whether ongoing or linked to a single event. The policy must apply to all staff, members of the management body, and members of the supervisory body, with particular attention to conflicts involving related parties and service providers. (cssf26_906eng.pdf, p.43)

The policy and procedures must require all actual and potential conflicts to be identified, assessed, managed, and either mitigated or avoided. They must identify the main sources of conflicts, the affected relationships and activities, and all internal and external parties involved, including relevant situations from the recent past that may still have an impact. The institution must assess the materiality of conflicts and determine how they are to be managed. Any remaining conflicts must be reported, documented, and managed to prevent unjustified consequences for the institution, its counterparties, or payment service users. Procedures must also address non-compliance with the policy. (cssf26_906eng.pdf, pp.43–44)

The institution must minimise conflicts through appropriate segregation of duties and activities, including controls over information access and the use of “Chinese walls.” It must also establish declaration, reporting, and escalation procedures. Staff must promptly and proactively inform their hierarchical superior of a conflict; management- and supervisory-body members must inform the relevant body. Persons conflicted, or unable to decide with full objectivity and independence, must abstain from the relevant decision-making. Internal control functions are responsible for identifying and managing conflicts of interest. (cssf26_906eng.pdf, p.44; cssf20_758eng.pdf, p.57)

For related-party transactions that may have a significant negative impact on the institution’s risk profile, whether individually or in aggregate, approval by the Board of Directors is required. (cssf20_758eng.pdf, p.57)

column2: what are the requirements for client asset segregation
column3:
Client assets must be adequately segregated and protected from the CASP’s proprietary assets. A CASP should place client assets in trust or otherwise segregate them, safeguard clients’ ownership rights, and prevent using client funds for its own account. Where appropriate, independent custodians or depositories should be used, particularly to reduce risks arising from the CASP’s insolvency. (FR_13_2025 Thematic Review Assessing the Implementation of IOSCO Recommendations for Crypto and Digital Asset Markets.pdf, pp. 52–53; Resolution on IOSCO Objectives and Principles of Securities Regulation and Methodology for Assessing Implementation of the IOSCO Objectives and Principles of Securities Regulation.pdf, p. 178; FR_13_2025 Thematic Review Assessing the Implementation of IOSCO Recommendations for Crypto and Digital Asset Markets.pdf, pp. 73–74)

The CASP must also maintain effective procedures to protect client assets against theft, fraud and other misappropriation. The excerpts give additional safeguards, including holding client assets on trust through a wholly owned associated entity, storing 98% of client crypto-assets in cold storage except where the regulator permits otherwise, and maintaining regulator-approved insurance or compensation arrangements covering specified potential losses. Clients must receive clear information about how assets and private keys are held, the use of independent, related-party or sub-custodians, any pooling or aggregation of assets and its risks, and risks connected with moving assets, including through a cross-chain bridge. (FR_13_2025 Thematic Review Assessing the Implementation of IOSCO Recommendations for Crypto and Digital Asset Markets.pdf, pp. 52–53, 73–74)

column2: what are the requirement for internal models for credit risk?
column3:
For credit risk, “internal models” means **IRB rating systems**. The excerpts require that:

- Each model be documented sufficiently for a qualified third party to understand and independently replicate its development and implementation. Documentation must cover the methodology and assumptions, data processes, user instructions, and performance and validation—including implementation-testing results. (ECB guide to internal models.pdf, pp. 9–10)
- The institution maintain a model register and documentation inventory. For each model, the register should record the owner(s), scope of application, materiality, approval date, use restrictions, key weaknesses, major changes and version history; third-party models must also be included. The register and inventory must be subject to adequate controls and an annual review. (ECB guide to internal models.pdf, pp. 9–10)
- A model risk management framework be in place, including a written policy, model-risk governance arrangements, a comprehensive model register, and guidelines for identifying and mitigating measurement uncertainty and model deficiencies according to their materiality. This must consider qualitative risks such as data deficiencies, model misuse and implementation errors. (ECB guide to internal models.pdf, pp. 11–12)
- Where external data are used for risk differentiation, risk quantification or review of estimates, the institution must know the data sources and the key processing applied to direct model-input variables, distinguish and document internal versus external data, and justify any modification of external data, selection of only part of a database, or use of a different provider. (ECB guide to internal models.pdf, pp. 101–102)

The excerpt also notes that using external bureau scores or ratings—especially as major inputs—may cause the model to omit relevant information, but it does not provide the specific mitigating principles in the supplied text. (ECB guide to internal models.pdf, p. 102)

column2: what are the ECB'S supervisory priorities for 2026-28?
column3:
The ECB’s supervisory priorities for 2026–28 are:

1. **Strengthening banks’ resilience to geopolitical risks and macro-financial uncertainties.** Banks are expected to apply prudent risk-taking and sound credit standards, implement **CRR III** consistently, and manage climate- and nature-related risks prudently. (ECB Annual Report on supervisory activities 2025.pdf, p.39)

2. **Strengthening operational resilience and ICT capabilities.** This includes complying with the new **DORA** requirements and promptly remedying deficiencies in risk-reporting capabilities and related information systems. (ECB Annual Report on supervisory activities 2025.pdf, p.39)

Under the second priority, the ECB is also developing a medium- to long-term supervisory focus on banks’ digital and AI-related strategies, governance and risk-management frameworks, including the structural trends and risk drivers that may shape the future of banking. (ECB Annual Report on supervisory activities 2025.pdf, p.39; Supervisory Priorities for 2026 - 2028 _ Management Solutions.pdf, p.1)

These priorities are based on the latest SREP results and are intended to address the sector’s main structural vulnerabilities while supporting consistent supervisory planning and resource allocation. (Supervisory Priorities for 2026 - 2028 _ Management Solutions.pdf, p.1; Supervisory priorities 2026-28.pdf, p.2-3)

column2: what are the SREP requirement for a bank?
column3:
Under the SREP, a bank is assessed on whether it maintains adequate capital over time from both a **normative** and an **economic** perspective. The assessment combines:

- a quantitative assessment of the bank’s capital risks; and  
- an assessment of its ICAAP, including the effectiveness of its capital-management strategies, methodologies and processes, and the quality of its baseline and adverse capital-planning scenarios and projections.  

The quantitative capital assessment is mandatory in every SREP cycle, while ICAAP aspects are assessed annually and through a multi-year assessment. The overall capital-adequacy score is based on both assessments and supervisory judgement. (SREP methodology for assessing capital adequacy.pdf, p.1)

More broadly, SREP determines the bank’s position against **capital and liquidity requirements** and assesses the adequacy of its internal governance and risk controls. It covers four elements: business model; governance and risk management; risks to capital; and risks to liquidity and funding. The SREP outcome may include applicable **Pillar 2 capital and liquidity quantitative requirements**, as well as additional qualitative measures. (Supervisory methodology 2025.pdf, p.1-2; Methodological note for the publication of aggregated Supervisory Banking Statistics.pdf, p.11)

The excerpts do not provide specific numerical capital thresholds or identify the precise legal basis for the requirements.

column2: what are the risk management requirements for a payment institution
column3:
A payment institution must maintain a risk-management framework comprising policies, procedures, limits, controls and alerts that enable the identification, measurement, management or mitigation, and reporting of risks. These arrangements must apply across operational units and the institution as a whole, including branches, subsidiaries, agents, distributors and representative offices. The framework must specifically cover capital adequacy, liquidity, management of payment flows, and the proper functioning of arrangements protecting payment-service users’ funds. (cssf26_906eng.pdf, p.38)

Where the institution grants credit linked to payment services, it must also have robust arrangements to detect, manage and report credit activity exceeding approved risk appetite or internal limits; manage the associated risks continuously so that capital and liquidity remain adequate in normal and crisis conditions; and identify and manage credit activities that have passed contractual or legal deadlines. (cssf26_906eng.pdf, p.38) For safeguarded funds invested in low-risk, liquid and secure assets, the institution must have a risk-management policy and monitor price volatility to ensure both ongoing safeguarding of users’ funds and sufficient liquidity for payment and electronic-money services. Foreign-exchange exposure should be minimised, or additional FX-protection mechanisms must be implemented where necessary. (cssf26_906eng.pdf, pp.48–49) Where safeguarding is provided through insurance or another guarantee, the management body must ensure that the guaranteed amount is reviewed regularly and remains sufficient to cover all relevant user funds. (cssf26_906eng.pdf, p.49)

column2: what are the AML/CFT requirements for a payment institution
column3:
A payment institution should be **licensed or registered and subject to effective AML/CFT compliance monitoring** in accordance with national requirements and the FATF Standards. Its AML/CFT controls should be proportionate to its money-laundering and terrorist-financing risk profile; supervisors should apply risk-based intensity and frequency to on-site and off-site supervision. Particular attention is warranted for cross-border activities and the use of agents, which may create significant inherent risks. (Recommendations for Regulating and Supervising Bank and Non-bank Payment Service Providers Offering Cross-border Payment Services_ Final report.pdf, pp. 23–24)

The institution should also address financial-crime risks when designing products, selecting delivery channels, introducing new technologies, or modifying existing products. For cross-border transfers, it must include the required and accurate originator and beneficiary information in the transfer or related messages and ensure that the information remains with the payment throughout the payment chain. (Recommendations for Regulating and Supervising Bank and Non-bank Payment Service Providers Offering Cross-border Payment Services_ Final report.pdf, pp. 23–24, 37)

Where the payment institution establishes cross-border correspondent or similar relationships, it should obtain information about the respondent institution, assess its AML/CFT controls, obtain senior-management approval before establishing the relationship, and clearly define each institution’s AML/CFT responsibilities. For payable-through accounts, it should ensure that the respondent has conducted customer due diligence on customers with direct access and can provide the relevant due-diligence information on request. (FATF Methodology 22 Feb 2013.pdf.coredownload.inline.pdf, pp. 51–52)

column2: what are the AML/CFT requirements for the ROA/CSSF questionnaire?
column3:
The excerpts do not define “ROA” specifically. For the CSSF AML/CFT questionnaire, the 2025 questionnaire collects standardised information on the ML/TF risks to which CSSF-supervised professionals are exposed and on the measures implemented to mitigate those risks. It must be submitted through the CSSF eDesk platform by **3 April 2026 at the latest**; the API transmission solution also remains available. (2025 Questionnaire on Financial Crime – CSSF.pdf, p.1)

Completion must be performed by the **RC** (compliance officer responsible for monitoring compliance with professional obligations) or the **RR** (person responsible for compliance with professional obligations). It may be delegated through eDesk to another employee or third party, but ultimate responsibility for adequate completion remains with the RC or RR. The RC/RR and any delegate must have an eDesk account authenticated through LuxTrust. (2025 Questionnaire on Financial Crime – CSSF.pdf, p.1)

For the underlying AML/CFT oversight, intermediaries are subject to **enhanced due diligence** from an AML and KYC perspective. Distributor due diligence must assess compliance with applicable AML/CTF laws and regulations, alongside marketing, governance and contractual requirements; it is generally performed through a distributor due-diligence questionnaire. (Delegate Due Diligence.pdf, pp.5–6)

column2: what are the requirements for a long form report (audit report)?
column3:
For financial years ending on or after **31 December 2024**, **all investment firms incorporated under Luxembourg law, including their branches, must prepare a Revised Long Form Report (RLFR)**. For the financial year ending 31 December 2023, the RLFR applied only to a sample of investment firms. (Publication of Circular CSSF 25_870 amending Circular CSSF 24_853 on the revised long form report for investment firms – CSSF.pdf, p.1)

The RLFR framework generally consists of **four dedicated reports**. However, investment firms subject to the RLFR for the first time from the year ending 31 December 2024 and presenting comparatively lower risk based on their risk attributes may qualify as **Partial Scope IFs**. These firms are subject to a proportionate, lighter framework and are currently required to submit **three dedicated reports**. They must also assess their compliance and the effectiveness of their internal organisational arrangements using the **RLFR self-assessment questionnaire (SAQ)**. (Publication of Circular CSSF 25_870 amending Circular CSSF 24_853 on the revised long form report for investment firms – CSSF.pdf, p.1)

column2: what are the depositary oversight requirements?
column3:
The depositary must generally be established in the same Member State as the AIF and must be an entity eligible under the AIFMD; the AIFM of the relevant AIF is expressly excluded to avoid conflicts of interest. Its responsibilities go beyond safekeeping and include oversight of the AIF, notably monitoring the AIF’s cash flows and covering the relevant activities of the AIF/AIFM. (EUR-Lex - 52021SC0340 - EN - EUR-Lex.pdf, p.154–155)

Only custody/safekeeping functions may be delegated. The depositary must retain responsibility for the necessary checks, including verifying that no financial instrument has been lost, and must ensure that information exchanged with the delegate through the custody chain is complete, timely and effective. Financial instruments held through the custody chain must be maintained in segregated financial-instrument accounts. The depositary generally remains liable to the AIF or its investors for loss of assets by a third party, subject to a valid discharge of liability or proof that the loss resulted from an external event beyond its reasonable control. (EUR-Lex - 52021SC0340 - EN - EUR-Lex.pdf, p.21–22; p.154–155)

The excerpts also identify an oversight gap concerning Central Securities Depositaries: under the AIFMD, a CSD is not treated as part of the custody chain or as the depositary’s delegate. This can hinder the depositary’s effective oversight because stable information on portfolio movements is not guaranteed, while CSDs follow CSDR asset-segregation rules rather than the more detailed rules applicable to custodial delegates. (EUR-Lex - 52021SC0340 - EN - EUR-Lex.pdf, p.21–22)

column2: quelles sont les exigences de la circulaire cssf 26/906?
column3:
La circulaire CSSF 26/906 s’applique aux établissements de paiement et aux établissements de monnaie électronique. Elle leur impose, afin d’assurer une gestion saine et prudente, de disposer d’un solide dispositif de gouvernance interne comprenant notamment : une structure organisationnelle claire, une répartition des responsabilités définie, transparente et cohérente, des processus efficaces d’identification, de gestion, de contrôle et de déclaration des risques, des mécanismes adéquats de contrôle interne — y compris des procédures administratives et comptables saines — ainsi que des mécanismes de contrôle et de sécurité des systèmes informatiques (cssf26_906.pdf, p. 1-2). La répartition des tâches doit respecter la ségrégation des tâches, mais la responsabilité au niveau de l’organe de gestion demeure collective (cssf26_906.pdf, p. 7-8).

L’application de ces exigences doit respecter le principe de proportionnalité. Les établissements doivent notamment tenir compte des risques et de la complexité de leurs produits et services, du volume des opérations de paiement et de monnaie électronique, de leur taille, du type et du nombre d’utilisateurs, du nombre d’employés, de l’étendue du réseau de distribution et de la taille du groupe auquel ils appartiennent. Les seuils indicatifs mentionnés sont notamment un volume supérieur à 10 milliards d’euros, un chiffre d’affaires ou total de bilan supérieur à 0,5 milliard d’euros, plus de 50 employés, ou un réseau comportant plusieurs succursales, agents, distributeurs ou bureaux de représentation (cssf26_906.pdf, p. 7-8).

Sur une base annuelle, l’établissement doit également fournir à la CSSF : l’évaluation des risques liés aux TIC et à la sécurité, l’attestation de conformité à la circulaire signée par tous les membres de l’organe de gestion, ainsi que les rapports de synthèse des fonctions de conformité et d’audit interne, signés respectivement par le Chief Compliance Officer et le Chief Internal Auditor. Ces documents doivent être soumis au plus tard le dernier jour du troisième mois suivant la clôture de l’exercice financier et peuvent être établis en français, allemand ou anglais (cssf26_906.pdf, p. 54-55). La circulaire est applicable à partir du 30 juin 2026 (cssf26_906.pdf, p. 54-55).

column2: what are the internal governance requirement for a financial institution?
column3:
Internal governance must ensure the sound and prudent management of the institution’s activities and inherent risks. It should include:

- A clear, consistent, transparent and complete organisational and operational structure, with well-defined decision-making powers, reporting and functional lines, allocation of responsibilities, and safeguards against conflicts of interest. (cssf26_906eng.pdf, p.8; cssf20_758eng.pdf, p.11-12)
- Adequate internal controls, including sound administrative, accounting and IT procedures; remuneration policies that support effective risk management; and control and security mechanisms for management information systems, including IT systems. (cssf26_906eng.pdf, p.8; cssf20_758eng.pdf, p.11-12)
- A formally defined risk-taking process and risk appetite covering all business areas and relevant risks, supported by rigorous decision-making, quality analysis and appropriate limits. Risks must be identified, measured, reported, managed, mitigated and controlled. (cssf26_906eng.pdf, p.8; cssf20_758eng.pdf, p.11-12)
- Formal procedures to escalate, resolve and, where appropriate, sanction problems, deficiencies and irregularities identified through internal controls or internal alert mechanisms. (cssf26_906eng.pdf, p.8)
- For payment and electronic money services, a clear structure covering agents, distributors, representative offices and branches, together with policies for their selection and oversight. It must also address money-laundering and terrorist-financing risks and operational and security risks related to those services. (cssf26_906eng.pdf, p.8)

The structure must not be unduly complex or impair the management body’s ability to manage and oversee the institution and its risks. Information necessary for sound management must be produced and distributed promptly, with significant management-information flows documented and available to the supervisory body, management body, internal control functions or competent authority on request. Complex structures and non-standard or potentially non-transparent activities require in-depth analysis and ongoing risk monitoring, including for financial-crime, money-laundering and terrorist-financing risks. (cssf26_906eng.pdf, p.43)

column2: what are the ECB's supervisory priorities for 2026-28 and how do they affect banks?
column3:
The ECB’s supervisory priorities for 2026–28 are organised around two main areas:

1. **Resilience to geopolitical and macro-financial risks:** banks are expected to apply prudent risk-taking and maintain sound credit standards, implement **CRR III** consistently, and manage climate- and nature-related risks prudently. (ECB Annual Report on supervisory activities 2025, p.39)

2. **Operational, ICT and digital resilience:** banks are expected to strengthen operational resilience and ICT capabilities, comply with the new **DORA** requirements, and remediate deficiencies in risk-reporting capabilities and related information systems in a timely manner. The ECB is also developing a medium- to long-term supervisory strategy covering banks’ digital and, particularly, AI-related strategies, governance and risk management. Targeted supervisory engagement on these themes is planned during 2026. (ECB Annual Report on supervisory activities 2025, p.39; Supervisory priorities 2026-28, pp.2–3)

For banks, this means that these areas will shape supervisory planning, resource allocation and ongoing engagement with Joint Supervisory Teams. Banks should expect continued follow-up on previous priorities and regulatory requirements, as well as risk-based supervisory action that may be adjusted annually in light of changes in the risk environment and SREP outcomes. The priorities are also intended to clarify supervisory expectations and promote consistent treatment across institutions; national supervisors will use them proportionately when setting priorities for less significant institutions. (Supervisory priorities 2026-28, pp.1, 2–3)

column2: what are the SREP capital requirements for a bank?
column3:
Under the SREP, a bank’s capital adequacy is assessed from both a **normative** and an **economic** perspective. The assessment combines a quantitative risk assessment with an assessment of the bank’s ICAAP—covering its capital-management strategies, methodologies, processes, and the quality of its baseline and adverse capital-planning scenarios—and is ultimately determined using supervisory judgement. The quantitative assessment is mandatory in every SREP cycle. (SREP methodology for assessing capital adequacy.pdf, p.1)

The excerpts do not provide a single capital requirement applicable to every bank; requirements are bank-specific. Across ECB-supervised banks, the **overall capital requirements and guidance** averaged **15.6% of risk-weighted assets** in both 2024 and 2025. The median **Pillar 2 capital requirement** was **2.2%** for the 2024 SREP and **2.3%** for the 2025 SREP. In 2025, average **Pillar 2 guidance** was **1.1%**, down from **1.3%** the previous year. Bank-specific Pillar 2 requirements, including requirements addressing excessive leverage, were made available for 2025 and 2026 respectively. (ECB Annual Report on supervisory activities 2024.pdf, pp.22–23; ECB Annual Report on supervisory activities 2025.pdf, pp.27–28)

column2: what are the requirements for internal models for credit risk?
column3:
For credit risk, “internal models” means **IRB rating systems**. They must be documented so that a qualified third party can independently understand and replicate their development and implementation, including the methodology, assumptions, limitations and intended use. Documentation should cover, at minimum, the model’s technical aspects, data processes, user instructions, performance and validation, including implementation-testing results. (ECB guide to internal models.pdf, pp.9–10)

Institutions must maintain a model register and documentation inventory, with adequate controls and at least an annual review. For each model, the register should identify the owner(s), application range, materiality, approval date, use restrictions, key weaknesses, significant changes and version history; third-party models must also be included. (ECB guide to internal models.pdf, pp.9–10) A model risk management framework should additionally include a written policy, clear governance arrangements covering model risk control, validation and internal audit, and procedures for identifying and mitigating measurement uncertainty and model deficiencies, including data deficiencies, misuse and implementation errors. (ECB guide to internal models.pdf, pp.11–12)

Where external data are used for risk differentiation, risk quantification or reviewing estimates, the institution must know the data sources and the main processing applied by the provider to direct model inputs. It must distinguish and document internal versus external data, and justify any modification of external data, selection of only part of an external database, or use of a different provider. (ECB guide to internal models.pdf, p.101)

column2: what are the ICAAP requirements for a bank?
column3:
A bank’s ICAAP must provide a sound, ongoing process to identify and manage its material risks and ensure that sufficient capital resources are available to cover those risks. Banks are expected to maintain adequate capital levels at all times. The ICAAP should be integrated into governance, internal controls and decision-making, including strategy and distribution decisions. (ICAAP_ enhanced supervisory assessment for stronger capital management in banks.pdf, p.1-3)

The ICAAP should cover four main areas:

- **ICAAP integration:** governance, controls and use of the ICAAP in decision-making, such as strategy and distributions;
- **Capital management:** capital planning, stress testing and management of capital adequacy from an economic perspective;
- **Risk controls:** management and quantification of risks to capital; and
- **Data quality and IT infrastructure.** (ICAAP_ enhanced supervisory assessment for stronger capital management in banks.pdf, p.1-3)

In practice, supervisors also expect capital planning frameworks to produce reliable capital projections under both baseline and adverse scenarios, supported by robust scenario design and stress testing. Banks must continuously improve their ICAAPs and related practices, including capital management, dividend and distribution policies, and coverage of risks from irrevocable payment commitments. (Aggregated results of the 2025 SREP.pdf, p.44-46) The excerpts identify the Capital Requirements Directive (CRD) as the legal basis but do not provide a specific article or detailed statutory requirement. (ICAAP_ enhanced supervisory assessment for stronger capital management in banks.pdf, p.1)

column2: what are the liquidity management tools under AIFMD?
column3:
The excerpts identify the following liquidity management tools (LMTs) associated with AIFMD/AIFs:

- **Suspension of subscriptions or redemptions**
- **Redemption gates** (quantitative limits on redemptions)
- **Side pockets**

(EUR-Lex - 52021SC0340 - EN - EUR-Lex.pdf, pp. 19–20) Soft closures and extensions of settlement periods are expressly said **not** to qualify as LMTs within the meaning of the AIFMD. column2: what are the UCITS sustainability requirements?
column3:
UCITS sustainability requirements are based on a **principles-based integration of sustainability risks**, rather than highly prescriptive rules. UCITS management companies should assess sustainability risks and take them into account in investment decision-making and risk management. Their governance, operating conditions and risk-management processes should be adapted accordingly. (esma34-45-688_final_report_on_integrating_sustainability_risks_and_factors_in_the_ucits_directive_and_the_aifmd.pdf, pp.10, 37–38)

In practical terms, the framework requires appropriate procedures and processes to ensure that sustainability-risk integration is effective, adequate and regularly reviewed; sufficient skills, expertise, knowledge, analytical support and resources; regular internal reporting; cooperation between relevant functions; and measures to identify, prevent, manage and disclose conflicts of interest arising from sustainability considerations. Systems and internal controls should also be adapted to sustainability risks. The governing body is responsible for the integration of sustainability risks and for periodically reviewing the risk-management policy, arrangements, processes, techniques and risk limits. (esma34-45-688_final_report_on_integrating_sustainability_risks_and_factors_in_the_ucits_directive_and_the_aifmd.pdf, pp.10, 14–15)

column2: what are the CSDR settlement discipline rules?
column3:
The CSDR settlement-discipline regime has three principal measures for addressing settlement fails:

- **Reporting and monitoring of settlement fails**;
- **Cash penalties** for settlement failures; and
- A **mandatory buy-in regime**.  
  (esma70-156-5011_final_report_-_rts_settlement_discipline_-_buy-in_suspension.pdf, p.5–6)

The framework also includes measures intended to **prevent settlement fails**, including allocations and confirmations, automation and reduced manual intervention, mandatory matching, and relevant CSD functionalities. It separately addresses the monitoring of fails, cash penalties, buy-ins, and participants that consistently and systematically fail. (2016-174_-_final_report_on_csdr_rts_on_settlement_discipline_0.pdf, p.1–2)

The settlement-discipline regime entered into force on **1 February 2022** after two postponements. Although market participants were considered largely ready for fail reporting and cash penalties, ESMA reported serious implementation difficulties concerning the buy-in regime. (esma70-156-5011_final_report_-_rts_settlement_discipline_-_buy-in_suspension.pdf, p.5–6) Subsequent policy discussion focused particularly on making the mandatory buy-in rules more proportionate and allowing different application dates for the separate settlement-discipline measures. (esma70-156-5011_final_report_-_rts_settlement_discipline_-_buy-in_suspension.pdf, p.12–13)

column2: what are the difference between pillar 2 guidance and pillar 2 requirement?
column3:
- **Pillar 2 Requirement (P2R):** An **additional own funds requirement imposed** under Article 104(1)(a) of Directive 2013/36/EU to address risks other than excessive leverage. It is therefore a formal capital requirement. (Final Report on revised SREP and supervisory stress testing Guidelines.pdf, p.27)

- **Pillar 2 Guidance (P2G):** The **level and quality of own funds the institution is expected to hold in excess of its overall capital requirement (OCR)**, determined using the supervisory criteria in the guidelines. The wording “expected to hold,” rather than “requirements imposed,” distinguishes P2G from P2R. (Final Report on revised SREP and supervisory stress testing Guidelines.pdf, p.27)

In short, **P2R is an imposed additional requirement**, while **P2G is an additional supervisory capital expectation above the OCR**. Both are reflected in discussions of banks’ overall capital requirements and guidance. (Understanding the EU banking sector’s capital framework.pdf, pp.5–6)

column2: What is the legal basis for the free movement of capital in the EU?
column3:
The primary legal basis is **Article 63 of the Treaty on the Functioning of the European Union (TFEU)**. It prohibits **all restrictions on movements of capital and payments between EU Member States and between Member States and third countries**. The provision has direct effect, meaning that it can confer rights on individuals who may rely on it before national courts, without implementing legislation. (Legal basis for the free movement of capital.pdf, p.1; Free movement of capital - Finance - European Commission.pdf, p.2–3)

The broader legal framework also includes **Treaty provisions, protocols and declarations, and transitional measures in accession acts**. Article 63 is subject to Treaty-based exceptions, including measures justified by taxation, prudential supervision of financial institutions, public policy, and security. The Court of Justice of the European Union has the final role in interpreting these provisions. (Free movement of capital - Finance - European Commission.pdf, p.2–3)

column2: What are the key requirements of the PRIIPs Regulation?
column3:
The excerpts indicate that the PRIIPs framework requires a **Key Information Document (KID)** for packaged retail and insurance-based investment products. The related technical standards govern the KID’s **presentation, content, review and revision**, as well as the conditions for providing it to investors (Revised Methodology on Value for Money Benchmarks.pdf, p.10).

Key information and cost-related requirements include:

- Investors must be informed of the **overall effect of costs and charges on investment returns**.
- Any anticipated **spikes or fluctuations in costs** must be shown, together with an explanation of the illustration.
- Firms distributing PRIIPs must disclose any **additional product costs or charges not included in the PRIIPs KID**, as well as costs and charges relating to the investment services provided (Delegated regulation - 2017_565 - EN - EUR-Lex.pdf, p.62).

The excerpts also link product governance to PRIIPs-related products: firms should identify the product’s target market and specify relevant **sustainability objectives**, such as minimum investments in environmentally sustainable or sustainable investments, consideration of principal adverse impacts, and an environmental, social or governance focus (ESMA35-43-3448_Guidelines_on_product_governance.pdf, pp.11–12).

column2: How is the MiFID II directive transposed into Luxembourg law?
column3:
The excerpts do not identify the specific Luxembourg legislation transposing **MiFID II**. They state only that MiFID II entered into force in January 2018. (EUR-Lex - 52021SC0340 - EN - EUR-Lex.pdf, pp. 9–10)

They describe Luxembourg’s earlier MiFID framework as being transposed through two national instruments: the **Law of 13 July 2007 on markets in financial instruments**, referred to as the “MiFID law,” transposing Directive 2004/39/EC, and the **Grand-Ducal Regulation of 13 July 2007 on organisational requirements and conduct of business rules in the financial sector**, transposing Commission Directive 2006/73/EC. Circular CSSF 07/307 explains and specifies those provisions; it must be read together with the law and regulation, which constitute the applicable conduct-of-business requirements. The framework requires institutions providing investment services to act honestly, fairly and professionally in the clients’ best interests. It also applies to relevant services or activities carried out by Luxembourg institutions in other EU Member States, subject to host-State rules for branches, and makes institutions fully responsible for their tied agents’ activities. column2: What are the ESMA guidelines on suitability?
column3:
ESMA’s suitability guidelines aim to improve clarity and promote consistent implementation of the relevant MiFID suitability requirements. When providing investment advice or portfolio management, an investment firm must ensure that each transaction recommended—or entered into for portfolio management—is suitable for the particular client or potential client. The guidelines are divided into General Guidelines and Supporting Guidelines and address only certain aspects of MiFID. (cssf07_307eng.pdf, p.100–101)

For crypto-asset services, ESMA’s suitability framework applies to the suitability requirements under Article 81 of MiCA. A “suitability assessment” means the complete process of collecting information about the client and assessing whether a crypto-asset is suitable, based on the crypto-asset service provider’s sound understanding of the crypto-assets it may recommend or invest in for the client. The same guidelines also address the format of periodic statements for providers conducting portfolio management of crypto-assets. (ESMA35-1872330276-2031_Guidelines_on_suitability_and_periodic_statement_MiCA.pdf, pp.5–6)

column2: How does ESMA's Q&A on MiFID II treat best execution?
column3:
The Q&A treats best execution as a **general, overarching obligation**. Firms must take **all reasonable steps to obtain the best possible result for clients**, considering price, costs, speed, likelihood of execution and settlement, order size, nature, and any other consideration relevant to execution. The requirement sets a high-level standard and gives firms considerable flexibility in how they comply, while still requiring compliance with specific provisions. (cssf07_307eng.pdf, p.59)

The Q&A identifies the relevant provisions as **Article 21 of Level 1** and **Articles 44 and 46 of Level 2**, with an indirect application through **Article 45(7)** for firms executing portfolio-management decisions. It covers firms that execute orders or decisions to deal, as well as firms that transmit or place orders with other entities for execution. (cssf07_307eng.pdf, pp.58–59) However, it expressly does **not** address the scope of best execution under MiFID or how it applies in dealer markets. CESR considered the Commission’s response sufficient for implementation and stated that no further work was needed at that time, while leaving open a possible future review of how the requirements were being applied. (cssf07_307eng.pdf, p.58)

column2: What is ESMA's supervisory briefing on outsourcing?
column3:
Based on the excerpts, ESMA’s outsourcing supervisory guidance is focused specifically on outsourcing to cloud service providers. It is intended to help firms and competent authorities identify, address and monitor risks throughout the outsourcing lifecycle—from deciding whether to outsource and selecting a provider, through monitoring the outsourced activities, to establishing exit strategies. (ESMA65-294529287-4737_Guidelines_on_outsourcing_to_cloud_service_providers.pdf, pp. 7–8)

The guidance expects competent authorities and firms to make every effort to comply. Competent authorities should incorporate it into their national legal or supervisory frameworks as appropriate and supervise firms’ compliance. They must notify ESMA within two months of publication whether they comply, intend to comply, or do not intend to comply, giving reasons in the last case; firms themselves are not required to submit such compliance notifications. column2: What work must the statutory auditor carry out in the event of an error in the calculation of the NAV according to CSSF Circular 24/856?
column3:
The statutory auditor (REA) must perform risk-based, sample-based controls over errors reported by the UCI as part of the separate report, covering the relevant financial year or audit period. The purpose is to verify that the conditions and remedial measures required by the Circular have been complied with (CSSF24_856eng.pdf, p.40).

For a **significant NAV calculation error**, the controls must cover:

- identifying the affected investors using the investor register;
- correcting the NAVs applied to subscription and/or redemption requests during the error period;
- calculating, using the corrected NAVs, the compensation payable to the UCI and/or investors for the loss suffered; and
- verifying that the compensation was actually paid in accordance with Section 7.2 (CSSF24_856eng.pdf, p.40).

Where the NAV error is classified as **another type of error**, the auditor must determine the compensation payable to the UCI and/or investors and verify that the method used to calculate the gains and/or losses is appropriate for the type of error (CSSF24_856eng.pdf, p.41).

column2: How should the fair value of a financial option be accounted for?
column3:
The fair value of a financial option should be measured using a suitable valuation technique, particularly where the option is thinly traded. The technique must reflect the option’s contractual terms and the fact that the holder is generally not entitled to dividends on the underlying equity during the option’s life. Relevant inputs for a European equity option include the risk-free discount curve, the underlying spot price, implied volatility, expected dividends or dividend yield, and the contractual terms. (Net Asset Valuation Calculation and Pricing Best Practice Guidelines.pdf, p.125; Net Asset Valuation Calculation and Pricing Best Practice Guidelines.pdf, pp.128–129)

For European call and put options, a risk-neutral Black–Scholes methodology may be used. The valuation should therefore incorporate the underlying price, strike price, time to expiration, discounting, volatility, and expected dividends. The option premium—the cost of entering into the contract—is usually paid upfront, but the excerpts do not specify separate journal entries or other accounting treatment for that premium. (Net Asset Valuation Calculation and Pricing Best Practice Guidelines.pdf, pp.128–129)

column2: How should financial statements be presented when the entity is not a going concern?
column3:
When an entity is facing imminent liquidation and is no longer a going concern, its financial statements should be prepared using the **liquidation basis of accounting**. The statements should focus on the cash and other resources expected to be available to satisfy obligations, rather than on going-concern operating results and cash flows. Assets should be measured at the cash amounts expected to be received on liquidation; they are not depreciated, and accumulated depreciation is not presented. Impairment testing and other going-concern valuation methods are no longer relevant. (Valuation and Reporting Issues Associated with a Liquidation Basis of Accounting - The CPA Journal.pdf, p.2; p.8)

Deferred charges, prepaid expenses, and other assets that will not be converted into cash or other consideration should be written off when the liquidation basis is adopted. Liabilities with specified contractual amounts should not be reduced to estimated settlement amounts until they are legally settled. The financial statements should also present the material information needed to understand the entity’s financial position and performance, with additional disclosures provided where the prescribed information is insufficient for users’ understanding. (Valuation and Reporting Issues Associated with a Liquidation Basis of Accounting - The CPA Journal.pdf, p.8; International Financial Reporting Standard 18Presentation and Disclosure in Financial Statements.pdf, p.8–9)

column2: What are the changes in accounting principles when a company is in liquidation?
column3:
When liquidation becomes imminent, the company moves from going-concern accounting to a liquidation basis; this is not an optional accounting policy choice. The financial statements change from a balance sheet, statement of comprehensive income, and cash-flow statement to a statement of net assets in liquidation and a statement of changes in net assets in liquidation. (Valuation and Reporting Issues Associated with a Liquidation Basis of Accounting, pp. 2–3)

The measurement focus also changes from normal going-concern recognition and measurement to expected liquidation proceeds and settlement amounts. All assets and liabilities must be recognized, including internally developed intangible assets if they are expected to be sold. (Valuation and Reporting Issues Associated with a Liquidation Basis of Accounting, p. 5) Under the liquidation framework described in the OIC 5 excerpt, tangible and intangible assets, equity investments, and debt securities are measured at the lower of their carrying amount at the start of liquidation and their realizable value; tangible and intangible assets are no longer depreciated, and debt securities are no longer measured using amortized cost. Receivables are measured at presumed realizable value, while liabilities are measured at presumed settlement value. Amortized-cost and discounting mechanisms generally do not apply because they are inconsistent with liquidation accounting. (OIC 5: key operational changes – valuation criteria and financial statements, p. 1) Before adopting the liquidation basis, assets and liabilities may also require adjustment to fair value, with goodwill tested using the specified net-assets-to-fair-value comparison. (Valuation and Reporting Issues Associated with a Liquidation Basis of Accounting, p. 5)

column2: What are the impacts of the new IFRS 18 standard on financial statements?
column3:
IFRS 18 is expected to change the **presentation and disclosure** of financial statements rather than how financial performance is measured. Its main impacts include new defined subtotals in the income statement, revised requirements for the aggregation and disaggregation of information, and disclosures concerning management-defined performance measures (MPMs). These changes are intended to improve the understandability and comparability of financial statements and provide investors with more consistent reference points for analysing performance. (IFRS 18 Presentation and Disclosure in Financial Statements - CBS Research Portal.pdf, pp.1–2; IFRS 18_ Introduction for Insurers.pdf, pp.4–5)

The changes may also affect reported key figures and ratios because the financial statements may be presented differently under IFRS 18. The impact will vary by entity and by the focus of the financial statement user; the excerpts indicate that comparability between entities may improve, while some ratios calculated without reformulating the balance sheet may not provide a fair basis, except for profit margin. Companies—particularly insurers—may need to adapt their financial-reporting processes, systems, internal and external communications, and coordination with auditors regarding judgements and MPM disclosures. (IFRS 18 Presentation and Disclosure in Financial Statements - CBS Research Portal.pdf, pp.1–2; IFRS 18_ Introduction for Insurers.pdf, pp.4–5)

column2: What are the impacts of the new law on securitisation in Luxembourg?
column3:
The excerpts do not identify or explain a specific **new securitisation law**, so they do not establish any direct changes to Luxembourg securitisation vehicles, transactions, or requirements.

They do, however, indicate the relevant regulatory perimeter for certain Luxembourg investment structures. The applicability of the Law of 30 March 1988 is assessed by examining the undertaking’s organisation and structure, including systematic share redemptions, investment-advisory arrangements, and fee arrangements. Financial investment companies formed for control purposes, family holding companies, and investment clubs are excluded in the stated circumstances because they do not constitute public collective investment of savings. (iml91_75eng.pdf, p.6–7) Luxembourg UCIs are classified according to their characteristics and may fall under Part I or Part II of that law. (iml91_75eng.pdf, p.6–7)

For UCITS, assets must generally be invested exclusively in transferable securities admitted to an official stock exchange or traded on a regularly operating, recognised and publicly open regulated market, subject to stated exceptions. (iml91_75eng.pdf, p.14–15) Separately, a CSSF circular applies to specified “Financial Entities,” including central securities depositories, management companies, investment fund managers, and alternative investment fund managers, as well as their branches. (cssf25_882eng.pdf, p.4) These excerpts therefore show potentially relevant fund and financial-sector rules, but do not provide a securitisation-specific impact or name the legal basis of the “new law.”

column2: How can the platform verify the consistency of data in a client's board management report
column3:
The platform can verify consistency by applying a structured data-quality methodology based on quantitative indicators and a management questionnaire. These checks should test whether the figures in the board management report are consistent with the underlying risk-data aggregation and risk-reporting processes, while flagging discrepancies caused by misunderstood reporting requirements, internal IT systems, third-party software, or operational and human errors. The results should be retained as evidence for management-body accountability. (ECB Annual Report on supervisory activities 2025.pdf, pp.64–65)

It should also perform reconciliations between selected disclosures in the report and the corresponding supervisory-reporting data, since the ECB’s annual reconciliation exercise produced improvements in data consistency and quality. Where issues are identified, the platform could support documented exchanges and remediation tracking through ASTRA, with the relevant supervisory authorities retaining access. (ECB Annual Report on supervisory activities 2025.pdf, pp.64–65) For any AI-enabled checks or claims in the report, it should require evidence-based substantiation, performance benchmarking where relevant, and disclosure of material reliance on third-party tools. (FR_02_2026 Supervisory Toolkit for AI Use in Capital Markets.pdf, pp.50–51) The excerpts do not specify a particular automated validation algorithm or a separate legal basis for these checks.

column2: What are the FATF's requirements for AML/CFT?
column3:
The FATF’s AML/CFT requirements are based on the **FATF Recommendations (2012)**, recognised as the global standard for combating money laundering and terrorist financing. Countries are assessed for **technical compliance**—whether the necessary laws, regulations and other measures are in force, and whether an appropriate AML/CFT institutional framework exists—and for **effectiveness**, meaning whether their AML/CFT systems operate in practice and achieve the defined outcomes. (FATF-4th-Round-Procedures.pdf.coredownload.pdf, pp.1–2, 5)

A core country obligation is to **identify and assess money-laundering and terrorist-financing risks on an ongoing basis**. The results must inform changes to the country’s AML/CFT regime, support the allocation and prioritisation of competent-authority resources in proportion to risk, and be made available to financial institutions and designated non-financial businesses and professions (DNFBPs) for their own risk assessments. (fatf-recommendations-2012.pdf, p.33) For proliferation financing, the FATF Standards’ requirements are limited to Recommendations 1, 2, 7 and 15; countries may exempt a financial institution or DNFBP from proliferation-financing risk-management requirements where the assessed risk is low, but targeted financial sanctions under Recommendation 7 remain mandatory in all cases. (fatf-recommendations-2012.pdf, p.33)

column2: What are the FATF's high-risk and monitored jurisdictions?
column3:
The excerpts do not provide the names of the FATF’s current high-risk or monitored jurisdictions. They describe them as jurisdictions with **strategic deficiencies in anti-money laundering, counter-terrorist financing and counter-proliferation financing (AML/CFT/CPF)** that present a risk to the international financial system and whose progress the FATF closely monitors through its International Co-operation Review Group (ICRG) process. (Report on the State of Effectiveness and Compliance with the FATF Standards.pdf, p.12)

A jurisdiction may enter this review process because it does not participate in a FATF-style regional body, fails to publish mutual-evaluation results in a timely manner, is nominated due to specific risks or threats, or has poor mutual-evaluation results. The FATF issues a public warning about risks from identified jurisdictions. To be removed from monitoring, a jurisdiction must address all or nearly all components of its action plan. column2: What are the main regulatory priorities for 2026 across EU authorities?
column3:
The **EBA’s 2026 priorities** are to: (1) develop a rulebook supporting an efficient, resilient and sustainable single market; (2) strengthen risk assessment through better tools, data and methodologies for analysis, supervision and oversight; and (3) address innovation to improve stakeholders’ technological capacity. It will also seek to simplify and improve the efficiency of the EU regulatory and supervisory framework, including Level 2 and Level 3 products, firms’ reporting costs, internal working arrangements and the wider prudential framework. (Executive summary work programme 2026.pdf, pp. 1–2) In addition, the EBA will expand oversight and supervisory work concerning critical third-party providers under DORA, issuers of crypto assets under MICA, and initial margin models under EMIR. (Executive summary work programme 2026.pdf, p. 1)

For **AMLA**, the central 2026 priority is convergence and consistency in the EU AML/CFT framework. Its main operational focus will be delivering six priority instruments for the private sector—through regulatory technical standards, implementing technical standards or guidelines—so that obliged entities have the tools to apply AML/CFT obligations consistently and effectively. (AMLA SPD 2026-2028.pdf, pp. 31–33) The excerpts also identify cooperation and inclusiveness, technology and innovation, and credibility and accountability as AMLA strategic priorities, alongside efforts to improve its own efficiency. (AMLA SPD 2026-2028.pdf, p. 31)

column2: What are the climate risk management expectations for financial institutions?
column3:
Financial institutions—particularly credit institutions—are expected to identify and assess climate-related and environmental risks as drivers of existing risk categories, including physical and transition risks that could materially affect their financial condition and operational capacity. They should understand the effects of these risks on their business environment over the short, medium and long term to support informed strategic and business decisions. (Circular 26_905.pdf, p.156; Good practices for climate and nature risk management.pdf, pp.76–77)

The management body should incorporate these risks into the institution’s overall business strategy, objectives and risk-management framework, and exercise effective oversight. Its collective suitability should include appropriate climate- and environmental-risk knowledge, skills and experience, while the relevant risk-management functions should receive adequate human and financial resources. (Good practices for climate and nature risk management.pdf, pp.45–46) Institutions should also maintain a holistic, documented view of the effects on all existing risk categories, covering on- and off-balance-sheet exposures, financial and non-financial risks, and both current and potential future exposures. They are expected to conduct regular processes to identify all material risks and record them in a comprehensive internal risk inventory. (Good practices for climate and nature risk management.pdf, pp.76–77) The Circular states that, following the application of the EBA Guidelines on the management of environmental, social and governance (ESG) risks (EBA/GL/2025/01), it remains applicable only to SNCIs until 10 January 2027 and to third-country branches. (Circular 26_905.pdf, p.156)

column2: What are the AML/CFT obligations for financial institutions?
column3:
Financial institutions must maintain the integrity of their AML/CFT frameworks and ensure that preventive measures are applied effectively. Their AML/CFT policies, controls and procedures should be proportionate to identified money-laundering and terrorist-financing risks; risk assessments should be properly conducted, documented and kept up to date. Measures should distinguish between higher- and lower-risk customers, relationships, transactions, products and countries, and CDD—including enhanced, simplified or specific measures—should vary according to risk. Where CDD is incomplete, the institution should assess whether the business relationship or transaction must be refused. Institutions should also ensure adequate access to relevant information by their AML/CFT compliance function and apply effective controls where reliance on third parties is used. (FATF-Assessment-Methodology-2022.pdf, pp. 137–138)

In relation to DeFi arrangements, institutions must assess the arrangement on a risk-based and proportionate basis and implement appropriate risk-mitigation measures. For centralised arrangements, they should conduct CDD, determine whether the arrangement is licensed or registered and adequately supervised, and perform sufficient due diligence or ensure that the arrangement has AML/CFT controls consistent with Recommendations 10 and 13. Where controllers cannot readily be identified, or where the arrangement is truly decentralised, they should apply appropriate AML/CFT measures to the underlying customers, including identity verification and, where appropriate, ongoing monitoring of the protocol’s integrity and security. They remain responsible for ensuring that their interactions with such arrangements comply with AML/CFT requirements. (targeted-report-decentralised-finance-2026.pdf.coredownload.pdf, p. 35)

column2: What are the data protection obligations under GDPR for financial institutions?
column3:
Financial institutions that profile customers or use automated decision-making must provide clear information about the processing. This includes explaining the processing to individuals, whether profiles will be shared with other organisations, the purposes for which a profile is used, and the source of information obtained from elsewhere. They must also present the right to object separately where applicable. These rights can be exercised against both the organisation creating the profile and the organisation making the automated decision, if they are different controllers. (5-guidelines-on-automated-individual-decision-making-and-profiling.pdf, pp.15–16)

They must implement appropriate technical and organisational measures when determining the processing methods and throughout the processing, integrating safeguards that effectively apply data-protection principles and protect individuals’ rights. They must also ensure security appropriate to the risk, considering the likelihood and severity of harm, including risks of unauthorised disclosure of or access to personal data. (edpb_bindingdecision_202301_ie_sa_facebooktransfers_en.pdf, p.38) A Data Protection Officer is mandatory where the institution’s core activities involve systematic, large-scale monitoring of individuals or large-scale processing of special categories of personal data; voluntary appointment may also be useful where the mandatory conditions do not apply. (8-guidelines-on-data-protection-officers-dpos.pdf, pp.3–4)

column2: Quelles sont les obligations de la circulaire CSSF 24/856 ?
column3:
La circulaire CSSF 24/856 impose aux professionnels de la gestion collective opérant au Luxembourg des lignes de conduite à appliquer lorsqu’une erreur survient dans l’administration ou la gestion d’un OPC, notamment une erreur de calcul de la valeur nette d’inventaire (VNI), un non-respect des règles de placement ou toute autre erreur couverte par la circulaire. Elle vise les OPC soumis à la surveillance de la CSSF, les gestionnaires de fonds d’investissement ainsi que les autres intervenants dans le fonctionnement et le contrôle de ces OPC. (cssf24_856.pdf, p.1-2)

L’administrateur d’OPC doit établir, mettre en œuvre et maintenir des procédures permettant de détecter, d’évaluer et, le cas échéant, de notifier sans délai les erreurs ou non-respects à l’OPC ou à son gestionnaire de fonds d’investissement. Ces incidents doivent être enregistrés, suivis et, lorsque nécessaire, corrigés après approbation de l’OPC ou de son gestionnaire. L’administrateur doit également élaborer, avec les autres intervenants, un plan de remédiation soumis à cette approbation, mettre en œuvre les mesures correctives et assurer un suivi approprié. La délégation de tâches ne le décharge pas de ses responsabilités : il doit notamment assurer une organisation adéquate englobant ses délégués. (cssf24_856.pdf, p.13-14)

Pour les fonds monétaires relevant de la circulaire, les lignes de conduite des chapitres 4 à 7 reposent notamment sur les pouvoirs de surveillance de la CSSF prévus par les articles 11 et 12 de la Loi ORE. L’article 38 du règlement MMF impose par ailleurs de veiller au respect des obligations du règlement, des documents constitutifs et du prospectus lorsqu’elles sont cohérentes avec ce règlement. (cssf24_856.pdf, p.9-10)

column2: What must be reported for an ICT-related incident under DORA?
column3:
Under DORA, financial entities must **record all ICT-related incidents and significant cyber threats**, but they are required to **report only major ICT-related incidents to the competent authorities**; non-major ICT-related incidents need not be reported to them. (Final Report on RTS Operational risk losses mandates.pdf, p.13)

For a major ICT-related incident, the report must include its **type**. The available categories are: **cybersecurity-related, process failure, system failure, external event, payment-related, or other** (with a specification). The incident is addressed through an initial notification, an intermediate report, and a final report, within the applicable time limits established by the relevant technical standards. The **loss or economic impact** must be reported **only in the final report**, due no later than one month after the intermediate report or, where applicable, the latest updated intermediate report. This must cover gross direct and indirect costs and losses incurred because of the incident, excluding financial recoveries and ordinary day-to-day operating costs such as general maintenance. (Final Report on RTS Operational risk losses mandates.pdf, p.13)
